What remains when integrability fails? Mathematical structure in the K(m,m)(m,m) compacton equations

James M. Hyman ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Tulane University, New Orleans, LA 70118, USA. Email: mhyman@tulane.edu.
Published in Discrete and Continuous Dynamical Systems, Series A,
Peter D. Lax Centennial Memorial Volume, doi:10.3934/dcds.2026.105536.
Author’s version, with the corrections made at proof.
Abstract

Peter Lax’s 1968 discovery that certain nonlinear wave equations possess operator pairs (Lax pairs) opened the theory of completely integrable systems, yielding exact solutions, infinite conservation hierarchies, and perfectly elastic soliton collisions. When a nonlinear dispersive equation is provably non-integrable (admitting no Lax pair and only finitely many conservation laws), what mathematical structure governs its dynamics?

The K(m,m) compacton equations, ut+(um)x+(um)x​x​x=0u_{t}+(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{m})_{xxx}=0 for m≥2m\geq 2, provide a testing ground: they support traveling waves with compact support, yet fail every known integrability test. We prove universal algebraic formulas determining the shape, width, and speed of every K(m,m) compacton. We develop a constraint-deficit mechanism explaining how the five independent conservation laws constrain emergent amplitudes and suppress the fundamental Fourier mode of the collision debris, while higher radiation modes remain unconstrained. The mechanism’s conclusions rest on explicit hypotheses supported by numerical evidence. A phase-plane analysis reveals the compacton as a singular limit of smooth solitary waves through simultaneous regularity loss and support compactification. These results delineate intermediate territory between integrable order and generic nonlinear dynamics, organized by scaling universality and by the constraint deficit of a finite conservation structure.

Dedicated to the memory of Peter D. Lax (1926–2025),
my teacher and friend, who introduced me to soliton theory
and whose search for organizing principles shaped a generation of mathematics

Keywords: Compactons, nonlinear dispersive equations, K(m,n) equations, conservation laws, non-integrability, Hamiltonian structure, quasi-elastic collisions, constraint deficit, singular limits, periodic waves.

Mathematics Subject Classification (2020): Primary 35Q53; Secondary 37K10, 35C07, 35B40, 35B65, 37J35.

1 Introduction

When does a nonlinear dispersive PDE possess systematic mathematical structure? For three decades following Lax’s 1968 discovery of operator-pair compatibility conditions for the Korteweg–de Vries equation [24, 23], the answer was clear: when the equation is completely integrable. The inverse scattering transform (IST) gave integrable systems a unified theory producing exact multi-soliton solutions, infinite conservation hierarchies, and algebraically determined collision outcomes [13, 1]. Equations outside the integrable class were treated as generic nonlinear problems requiring ad hoc numerical investigation. Often implicitly, the field operated with a dichotomy: integrable equations possess mathematical structure, and everything else does not. This paper presents evidence that the dichotomy is incomplete.

Our evidence comes from the K(m,n) family of nonlinear dispersive equations,

ut+(um)x+(un)x​x​x=0,u_{t}+(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{n})_{xxx}=0, (1)

introduced in 1993 [15]. Rosenau was the first to conceive the K(m,n) equations and to unfold their special properties, and he went on to make major advances in understanding them [38, 39, 40, 41, 42, 17]. The case K(2,1) recovers KdV, and K(3,1) corresponds to the modified KdV equation after scaling; these are the only integrable members of the family with a standard polynomial nonlinearity [8]. (Exotic integrable cases with negative exponents, such as K(−2,−2)(-2,-2) and K(−1/2,−1/2)(-1/2,-1/2), arise in the tri-Hamiltonian duality of Olver and Rosenau [38] but lie outside the scope of this paper.) Equal convective and dispersive exponents (m=nm=n) with m>1m>1 are sufficient for equation (1) to admit traveling wave solutions with genuinely compact support: compactons, which vanish identically beyond a finite boundary rather than decaying exponentially. The mechanism enabling compact support is the amplitude-dependent dispersion in the term (um)x​x​x(u^{m})_{xxx}, which degenerates where u→0u\to 0 and cannot sustain exponential tails. The exponent mm need not be an integer for compacton existence; for non-integer mm, the absolute-value formulation |u|m−1​u|u|^{m-1}u extends the equation to solutions that may change sign [5]. All K(m,m) equations with real m>1m>1 are provably non-integrable; on the diagonal m=nm=n, compactification and non-integrability are coextensive.

What is surprising is what these non-integrable equations possess. K(m,m) compactons satisfy universal algebraic formulas connecting the three compacton parameters (the edge regularity exponent α\alpha, the width parameter ℓ\ell, and the speed cc) to the single nonlinearity exponent mm. Specifically, K(m,m) compactons take the form

u⁡(x,t)=A​cosα⁡(x−c​tℓ),|x−c​t|≤π​ℓ2,u(x,t)=A\cos^{\alpha}\!\!\left(\frac{x-ct}{\ell}\right),\qquad|x-ct|\leq\tfrac{\pi\ell}{2},

vanishing identically outside this interval, where α\alpha governs the rate of approach to zero at the support boundary. We prove (Theorem 4.1) that for all m>1m>1:

α=2m−1,ℓ=2​mm−1,c=m+12​m​Am−1.\alpha=\frac{2}{m-1},\qquad\ell=\frac{2m}{m-1},\qquad c=\frac{m+1}{2m}\,A^{m-1}. (2)

These formulas were identified through pattern recognition across individual cases m=2,…,7m=2,\ldots,7 [15, 39, 8, 17], but their status had remained that of empirical regularities. The proof establishes them as algebraic consequences of the cosine-power ansatz and the traveling wave ODE, valid for all real m>1m>1.

These universal formulas are one component of a richer mathematical picture. The K(m,m) equations possess five known independent conservation laws (exactly four local [46] and one nonlocal [17]), a count lying strictly between the two conservation laws (mass and energy) that generic Hamiltonian PDEs possess and the infinite hierarchy of integrable systems. The equations admit single Hamiltonian structure but not the bi-Hamiltonian pair required for Magri’s recursion operator [29]. Compacton collisions are quasi-elastic [15, 17]: in the collisions computed here the emerging waves keep their amplitudes to within 0.5%0.5\%, and a small-amplitude debris field carries the remainder (§5.1). This is not residual integrability. It is a different kind of mathematical order, governed by a finite conservation structure rather than an infinite one.

This paper makes three contributions.

First, we synthesize the universal formulas, conservation structure, Hamiltonian geometry, and collision mechanics of K(m,m) compactons into a coherent mathematical framework. The individual components have been developed separately [15, 39, 46, 8, 17]; bringing them together reveals their interconnections and the pattern they form.

Second, we prove results that sharpen the framework. Theorem 4.1 provides a unified derivation of the universal formulas for all m>1m>1; the individual formulas appear in the literature [15, 17], but their simultaneous emergence from a single traveling-wave analysis appears to be new. This derivation yields consequences that had not been previously identified: a trigonometric orthogonality property, monotonicity of the mass and of the translation generator along the compacton family (Corollary 4.5), and the exclusivity of the cosine-power ansatz to the K(m,m) subfamily. Theorem 5.1, under hypotheses (H1)–(H3) supported by numerical evidence, identifies a mechanism behind imperfect collision elasticity in the K(m,m) family: the five conservation laws constrain emergent amplitudes and force the fundamental Fourier mode of collision debris to vanish, but leave all higher radiation modes unconstrained. Numerical spectral analysis across the family confirms this prediction: post-collision debris exhibits a characteristic notch at wavenumber k=1k=1 for all tested values of mm. This constraint-deficit framework is introduced here; it explains both the algebraic order (why universal formulas exist) and the dynamical imperfection (why K(m,m) collisions are near-elastic but not exactly elastic).

Third, we propose a conservation–elasticity framework (Conjecture 5.7) relating collision elasticity to both the conservation law count and the interaction geometry of solitary waves. Quantitative comparison of collisions in K(m,m) and in the Benjamin–Bona–Mahony (BBM) equation [5], using identical methodology, shows that BBM solitary waves (N=3N=3 known conservation laws, smooth exponential tails) collide about as elastically as K(m,m) compactons (N=5N=5 conservation laws, compact support) by the amplitude measure, while shedding more debris energy. Whether interaction geometry modulates the role of the conservation law count therefore remains open. We also pose eight open problems defining a research program for investigating mathematical structure in K(m,m) and in other non-integrable systems (Appendix K).

An arc runs through this paper, from Lax’s integrable vision through its failure for K(m,m) to what replaces it. The author had the privilege of being Peter Lax’s student, colleague, and friend, and this contribution continues a conversation about structure in nonlinear waves that began in his office at the Courant Institute. Lax’s contributions to nonlinear wave theory extended well beyond the operator-pair construction [27]: his broader program sought organizing principles for nonlinear PDEs wherever such principles might exist. For KdV and its integrable relatives, the IST remains the organizing principle. For K(m,m), a different organizing principle operates: scaling universality and finite conservation structure produce systematic, predictable behavior without recourse to spectral theory.

Figure 1 provides a conceptual roadmap for the paper’s argument.

Section 2 reviews the integrable paradigm, presenting Lax pairs, the IST, and the four structural features of integrable systems that will serve as reference points throughout. Section 3 introduces the K(m,m) compacton family and establishes non-integrability through four independent lines of evidence. Section 4 presents the universal formulas with their proof, the regularity classification, the finite conservation hierarchy, and Hamiltonian geometry. Section 5 develops the collision theory, constraint-deficit mechanism, and BBM comparison, concluding with broader implications of the constraint-deficit framework for non-integrable dispersive PDEs. Section 6 examines compacton emergence from localized initial data, demonstrating that the universal speed formula is recovered to within one percent in dynamics that begin far from any compacton profile, and identifying a resolution limit controlled by the boundary regularity exponent α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1). Section 7 reveals a phase-plane bifurcation governed by a critical speed and identifies the compacton as a singular limit of smooth waves, providing a precise connection to Lax’s 1975 periodic KdV theory [25]. Eight concrete open problems are posed in Appendix K, with extended versions in the Supplement. Detailed derivations and extended numerical results appear in Appendices A–K below; computational data, simulation code, and reproducibility materials are collected in the accompanying computational supplement. Readers familiar with the integrable paradigm may proceed from Section 1 directly to Section 3; the contributions of this paper begin in Section 4.

Notation.

Throughout, mm and nn denote the nonlinearity exponents in the K(m,n) family (1). The compacton existence results (Theorem 4.1) and non-integrability (§3) hold for all real m>1m>1; the conservation law, Hamiltonian, and collision analyses (§§4.3–5.1) are established for integer m≥2m\geq 2. For traveling waves, ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct is the co-moving coordinate, c>0c>0 the propagation speed, and A>0A>0 the amplitude. The compacton profile parameters are the edge exponent α\alpha, the width parameter ℓ\ell (so that the support is |ξ|≤π​ℓ/2|\xi|\leq\pi\ell/2), and the speed coefficient k⁡(m)=c/Am−1k(m)=c/A^{m-1}. Conservation integrals are labeled I0,…,I4I_{0},\ldots,I_{4} following the ordering in §4.3.

2 The integrable paradigm

Few developments in twentieth-century mathematics have been as surprising as the discovery that certain nonlinear PDEs possess hidden linear structure. The story begins with a numerical accident: Fermi, Pasta, Ulam, and Tsingou observed unexpected recurrence in a nonlinear lattice [11]. Zabusky and Kruskal traced the recurrence to particle-like waves that survive mutual collisions intact [47]. Gardner, Greene, Kruskal, and Miura then showed that the Korteweg–de Vries equation could be solved exactly by an inverse scattering method [13], and Lax distilled the mechanism to its algebraic essence: an operator pair whose compatibility condition is equivalent to the PDE [24]. This section reviews the integrable framework that emerged from these discoveries, emphasizing the specific features that will serve as reference points when we examine the K(m,m) family in Sections 3 and 4.

2.1 Lax pairs and the KdV archetype

The KdV equation, written in K(2,1) normalization as

ut+(u2)x+ux​x​x=0,u_{t}+(u^{2})_{x}+u_{xxx}=0, (3)

balances nonlinear convection (u2)x=2​u​ux(u^{2})_{x}=2uu_{x} against linear dispersion ux​x​xu_{xxx}. Its soliton solutions

u⁡(x,t)=6​κ2​sech2⁡(κ⁡(x−4​κ2​t))u(x,t)=6\kappa^{2}\operatorname{sech}^{2}\bigl(\kappa(x-4\kappa^{2}t)\bigr) (4)

decay exponentially as |x|→∞|x|\to\infty, propagate at speed c=4​κ2c=4\kappa^{2} proportional to the amplitude A=6​κ2A=6\kappa^{2}, and interact elastically: two solitons emerge from a collision with their shapes and speeds intact, displaced only by a phase shift [47].

These properties are not coincidental. They follow from a deep structural fact discovered by Lax [24]: KdV admits a Lax pair representation. Associated with equation (3) are two linear operators,

L=−∂x2+13u,M=−4∂x3+2u∂x+ux,L=-\partial_{x}^{2}+\tfrac{1}{3}u,\qquad M=-4\partial_{x}^{3}+2u\,\partial_{x}+u_{x}, (5)

whose compatibility condition Lt=[M,L]L_{t}=[M,L] is equivalent to the nonlinear PDE. The operator LL is a Schrödinger eigenvalue problem (with potential u/3u/3); MM governs the time evolution of the eigenfunctions. Together they convert a nonlinear initial-value problem into a sequence of linear operations: decompose initial data into spectral components of LL, evolve these components linearly through MM, and reconstruct the solution at any later time through the inverse scattering transform [13, 1].

The geometric content of this construction deserves emphasis. The Lax equation Lt=[M,L]L_{t}=[M,L] asserts that the spectrum of LL is preserved under the time evolution defined by MM. KdV dynamics are isospectral deformations: the potential in LL changes, but its eigenvalues remain fixed. Each eigenvalue corresponds to a soliton, and spectral invariance explains why solitons retain their identities through interactions. The phase shift experienced during collision is encoded in the scattering matrix, which evolves linearly in the IST framework [1].

This is not merely a technique for solving KdV. It reveals that the equation possesses an organizing principle, namely spectral theory, governing its entire solution space. Multi-soliton solutions follow from NN-fold Darboux transformations or Hirota’s bilinear method [20], both deriving from the same Lax pair structure. The organizing principle is algebraic: the spectral data form a complete set of coordinates in which KdV becomes a linear flow.

2.2 What integrability buys

The Lax pair structure ramifies into four concrete mathematical consequences, each of which plays a distinct role in the theory of integrable dispersive equations.

An infinite conservation hierarchy.

Lax [24] showed that the isospectral property generates an infinite sequence of conserved quantities I0,I1,I2,…I_{0},I_{1},I_{2},\ldots for KdV (in this section only; from §4.3 on, I0,…,I4I_{0},\ldots,I_{4} denote the K(m,m) laws). The first three have direct physical interpretations: mass I0=∫u​𝑑xI_{0}=\int u\,dx, momentum I1=∫u2​𝑑xI_{1}=\int u^{2}\,dx, and energy I2=∫(13​u3−12​ux2)​𝑑xI_{2}=\int(\tfrac{1}{3}u^{3}-\tfrac{1}{2}u_{x}^{2})\,dx. Higher conservation laws involve progressively complex differential expressions, but the sequence continues without termination.

These infinitely many constraints overdetermine the dynamics in a precise sense. For a system with NN solitons, NN spectral parameters characterize the solution completely. The infinite conservation laws provide far more than NN constraints, encoding not only the discrete spectrum (soliton parameters) but also the continuous spectrum (radiation). Complete integrability means that the conservation laws form a maximal involutive set under the Poisson bracket, in the sense of Liouville–Arnold theory [3].

Perfectly elastic collisions.

When two KdV solitons collide, both emerge with exactly their pre-collision amplitudes, speeds, and shapes. The only trace of the interaction is a phase shift: each soliton is displaced from where it would have been without the encounter. No radiation is generated, no energy is lost to dispersive tails, and no amplitude change occurs. This perfect elasticity holds for any number of simultaneously interacting solitons and is a direct consequence of the IST: spectral data are preserved under the nonlinear evolution, so the asymptotic soliton parameters cannot change [1].

Bi-Hamiltonian structure.

Magri [29] and Fokas and Fuchssteiner [12] discovered that KdV admits not one but two compatible Hamiltonian formulations. Two Poisson operators

𝒥1=−∂x,𝒥2=−∂x3−23(u∂x+∂xu)\mathcal{J}_{1}=-\partial_{x},\qquad\mathcal{J}_{2}=-\partial_{x}^{3}-\tfrac{2}{3}(u\,\partial_{x}+\partial_{x}\,u) (6)

generate the same dynamics through different Hamiltonians: ut=𝒥1​δ​H1/δ​u=𝒥2​δ​H2/δ​uu_{t}=\mathcal{J}_{1}\,\delta H_{1}/\delta u=\mathcal{J}_{2}\,\delta H_{2}/\delta u, where H1=∫(13​u3−12​ux2)​𝑑xH_{1}=\int(\tfrac{1}{3}u^{3}-\tfrac{1}{2}u_{x}^{2})\,dx and H2=12​∫u2​𝑑xH_{2}=\tfrac{1}{2}\!\int u^{2}\,dx. The recursion operator ℛ=𝒥2​𝒥1−1\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{J}_{2}\,\mathcal{J}_{1}^{-1} produces the infinite conservation hierarchy automatically through the Lenard scheme [29, 12], connecting conservation laws at successive differential orders. Bi-Hamiltonian structure is not merely a reformulation; it provides the mechanism generating the infinite hierarchy.

Exact multi-soliton formulas.

The IST yields closed-form NN-soliton solutions through Hirota’s bilinear method [20] or the Gel’fand–Levitan–Marchenko integral equation [1], expressing the complete NN-body interaction algebraically in terms of spectral parameters.

Together, these four features constitute the integrable paradigm: spectral theory organizes the entire solution space through conservation laws, elastic collisions, bi-Hamiltonian geometry, and exact formulas.

2.3 The prevailing dichotomy

The integrable paradigm has shaped how the nonlinear dispersive wave community organizes its subject. Textbooks tend to divide their material into integrable equations (treated analytically) and non-integrable equations (treated numerically) [1, 10]. An implicit assumption pervades the field: equations either possess the full integrable apparatus or they lack systematic analytical theory altogether. Equations admitting Lax pairs receive extensive analytical attention; those failing the Painlevé test or the bi-Hamiltonian criterion are often relegated to numerical simulation.

The K(m,m) compacton family challenges this dichotomy fundamentally. The challenge is sharpened by recent work of Anco and Gandarias [2], who developed a rigorous weak (distributional) formulation for compacton solutions of nonlinearly dispersive KdV-type equations. Their framework establishes that compactons (which may fail to be classical solutions at the support boundary) satisfy the PDE in a precise distributional sense. This places the analytical theory of non-integrable compacton equations on firmer ground: the structures developed in the following sections rest on a well-defined solution concept rather than purely formal manipulations. As the next section demonstrates, these equations fail every standard test of integrability, yet the mathematical structure they exhibit cannot be dismissed as coincidence.

3 The K(m,m) family: non-integrability established

This section surveys established results on K(m,m) non-integrability: the compacton construction [15], the integrability classification of Hernández Heredero et al. [8], and Vodová’s conservation law analysis [46]. The contribution here is not new theorems but a unified presentation connecting these results to the paper’s main theme: what mathematical structure persists when integrability fails.

The generalized KdV family

ut+(um)x+(un)x​x​x=0,m,n>1,u_{t}+(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{n})_{xxx}=0,\qquad m,n>1, (7)

introduced in [15], provides an ideal test case. This two-parameter extension of KdV allows both the convective and dispersive nonlinearities to be independently specified. When m=2m=2 and n=1n=1, equation (7) reduces to the classical KdV. When m=nm=n, a qualitatively new phenomenon appears: solitary waves with genuinely compact support.

3.1 Compactons: a new kind of localization

Consider the K(m,m) equation

ut+(um)x+(um)x​x​x=0,m>1.u_{t}+(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{m})_{xxx}=0,\qquad m>1. (8)

The critical distinction from KdV lies in the dispersive term (um)x​x​x(u^{m})_{xxx}. In KdV, the linear dispersion ux​x​xu_{xxx} operates at all amplitudes: even where uu is negligibly small, dispersive spreading persists. In K(m,m), the dispersive strength scales as um−1u^{m-1}, vanishing wherever the solution vanishes. When dispersion shuts off at u=0u=0, nothing prevents the solution from remaining identically zero beyond a finite boundary. Compact support arises not from artificial truncation or imposed boundary conditions, but from the intrinsic structure of the equation.

This mechanism produces compactons: solitary waves that vanish identically outside a finite interval [15]. The term, coined by Rosenau, reflects the compact support that distinguishes these waves from classical solitons. Amplitude-dependent dispersion and the resulting compact support also arises in the dynamics of granular chains [11, 12], giving the K(m,n) family physical as well as mathematical interest. Subsequent investigations by Rosenau [40, 41, 42] explored the analytical properties of these nonanalytic solutions and their role within broader families of nonlinear dispersive interactions.

To make the compact support mechanism concrete, consider the traveling wave reduction. Substituting u⁡(x,t)=U⁡(x−c​t)u(x,t)=U(x-ct) into equation (8) and integrating once yields the ODE

−c​U+Um+(Um)′′=0,-cU+U^{m}+(U^{m})^{\prime\prime}=0, (9)

where primes denote derivatives with respect to ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct. At any point where U=0U=0, the nonlinear terms vanish: the equation becomes 0+0+0=00+0+0=0, satisfied trivially. A solution that reaches U=0U=0 at some finite ξ0\xi_{0} can continue as U≡0U\equiv 0 for all |ξ|>ξ0|\xi|>\xi_{0} without violating the equation. No exponential tail is forced, because no linear mechanism drives the solution away from zero. The general ansatz U⁡(ξ)=A​cosα⁡(ξ/ℓ)U(\xi)=A\cos^{\alpha}(\xi/\ell) for |ξ|≤π​ℓ/2|\xi|\leq\pi\ell/2 captures this structure, with the three parameters α\alpha, ℓ\ell, and AA determined by the ODE.

K(2,2).

The simplest case, ut+(u2)x+(u2)x​x​x=0u_{t}+(u^{2})_{x}+(u^{2})_{xxx}=0, admits traveling wave solutions of the form

u⁡(x,t)=4​c3​cos2⁡(x−c​t4)for ​|x−c​t|≤2​π,u(x,t)=\frac{4c}{3}\cos^{2}\!\biggl(\frac{x-ct}{4}\biggr)\quad\text{for }|x-ct|\leq 2\pi, (10)

and u≡0u\equiv 0 elsewhere. The amplitude is A=4​c/3A=4c/3 and the speed–amplitude relation is c=(3/4)​Ac=(3/4)A, linear in amplitude. The solution vanishes quadratically at its edges: near the boundary ξ0=2​π\xi_{0}=2\pi, the profile behaves as u∼B​(ξ0−ξ)2u\sim B(\xi_{0}-\xi)^{2}, maintaining continuous first derivatives at the junction with the exterior zero state. The support has fixed width 4​π4\pi, independent of amplitude [15].

K(3,3).

Cubic nonlinearity changes the edge character. The equation ut+(u3)x+(u3)x​x​x=0u_{t}+(u^{3})_{x}+(u^{3})_{xxx}=0 admits

u⁡(x,t)=A​cos⁡(x−c​t3)for ​|x−c​t|≤3​π2,u(x,t)=A\cos\!\biggl(\frac{x-ct}{3}\biggr)\quad\text{for }|x-ct|\leq\frac{3\pi}{2}, (11)

with c=(2/3)​A2c=(2/3)A^{2}. The edge exponent drops to α=1\alpha=1: the solution vanishes linearly, producing cusp-like boundaries where the first derivative jumps discontinuously [39]. Despite this reduced regularity, the compacton propagates without change of form and retains its compact support indefinitely. The support width is 3​π3\pi, narrower than 4​π4\pi for K(2,2), again independent of amplitude. The quadratic speed–amplitude relation c=(2/3)​A2c=(2/3)A^{2} means that K(3,3) compactons of different amplitudes separate more rapidly than their K(2,2) counterparts, where the relation is linear.

K(4,4) and beyond.

The pattern continues with increasing nonlinearity. K(4,4) admits solutions u=A​cos2/3⁡(ξ/ℓ)u=A\cos^{2/3}(\xi/\ell) with fractional edge exponent α=2/3\alpha=2/3 and support width (8/3)​π(8/3)\pi. Derivatives diverge at the boundary, requiring weak solution formulations for mathematical rigor [17]. Subsequent cases K(5,5) through K(7,7) exhibit progressively sharper edges (with α=1/2,2/5,1/3\alpha=1/2,2/5,1/3 respectively) while maintaining the same compact support structure. Cooper, Shepard, and Sodano [9] studied these generalized solitary wave solutions within a broader class of KdV-type equations, confirming the systematic parameter relationships across the family.

Figure 2 displays representative compacton profiles for K(2,2), K(3,3), and K(4,4), each with unit amplitude. The regularity transition is visible at the support boundary: K(2,2) joins the zero exterior smoothly with vanishing slope, K(3,3) meets it at a cusp with nonzero slope, and K(4,4) arrives with diverging derivative. All three profiles have the cosine-power form U⁡(ξ)=cosα⁡(ξ/ℓ)U(\xi)=\cos^{\alpha}(\xi/\ell) from the traveling wave ansatz, with the amplitude-independent widths W=π​ℓW=\pi\ell decreasing as mm increases.

Three features distinguish compactons from KdV solitons. First, compactons vanish identically beyond a finite boundary determined by the equation structure, rather than decaying exponentially over infinite extent. Second, their spatial width is amplitude-independent: all K(m,m) compactons of a given mm occupy the same interval regardless of how tall they are. Third, edge regularity depends on mm, transitioning from smooth (m=2m=2) through cusped (m=3m=3) to singular-derivative (m≥4m\geq 4).

3.2 The Hernández Heredero–Euler–Reyes classification

Given these striking traveling wave solutions, a natural question arises: might K(m,m) equations be integrable despite their departure from KdV? Could some hidden Lax pair or recursion operator exist, restoring the full integrable apparatus?

The definitive answer is no. Hernández Heredero, Euler, Euler, and Reyes [8] resolved the integrability question for the entire K(m,n) family through a systematic analysis of formal symmetry structure.

Their classification is exhaustive: integrable K(m,n) equations exist only when the dispersive exponent takes one of three values, n∈{1,−2,−12}n\in\{1,\;-2,\;-\tfrac{1}{2}\}, with a finite list of admissible convective exponents mm in each case. These include the familiar K(2,1) = KdV and K(3,1) ∼\sim mKdV (related through a Miura-type transformation [32]) on the n=1n=1 line, together with exotic negative-exponent cases such as K(−2-2,−2-2), K(−12-\tfrac{1}{2},−12-\tfrac{1}{2}), and K(−1-1,−2-2) that are connected to KdV through nonlocal differential substitutions. We extract the consequence relevant to the present work.

Theorem 3.1 (Non-integrability of compacton equations [8]).

No K(m,n) equation (7) with m>1m>1 and n>1n>1 possesses a recursion operator. In particular, no such equation is completely integrable.

Proof.

The Hernández Heredero–Euler–Reyes classification proves that K(m,n) admits a recursion operator only when n∈{1,−2,−12}n\in\{1,-2,-\frac{1}{2}\}. Since n>1n>1 excludes all three values, the result follows immediately. ∎

The proof of the full classification proceeds through compatibility conditions for formal recursion operators acting on symmetry spaces. For integrable equations, these conditions hold at every differential order. For non-integrable cases, contradictions emerge at finite order, terminating the symmetry hierarchy.

The critical consequence for the present work is this: every K(m,m) equation with real m>1m>1 is non-integrable. On the diagonal m=nm=n the only integrable members are m=−2m=-2 and m=−12m=-\frac{1}{2}, both with negative exponents and no compacton solutions, together with the degenerate linear case m=1m=1. Because the classification treats mm and nn as real parameters (note the non-integer integrable case m=−12m=-\frac{1}{2}), the conclusion holds for all real m>1m>1, not merely for integers. The matched nonlinearity, with dispersion power equal to convection power, yields compactons and also destroys integrability: no K(m,m) equation supports both compact solitary waves and the algebraic machinery of complete integrability.

All integrable K(m,n) equations are connected to KdV through differential substitutions, establishing K(2,1) as the archetypal progenitor of the integrable subfamily. K(m,m) equations with m>1m>1, by contrast, stand isolated: no Miura-type transformation connects them to any integrable system [8]. This isolation is not merely the absence of a known transformation. The Hernández Heredero–Euler–Reyes analysis proves that no such transformation can exist, because the underlying symmetry structure is incompatible with infinite-dimensional recursion.

3.3 Four proofs of non-integrability

The classification theorem settles the question through formal symmetry methods. But K(m,m) non-integrability is overdetermined: four independent lines of evidence converge on the same conclusion.

(a) Finite conservation hierarchy.

Vodová [46] proved structurally that K(m,m) equations with m≠−2,−1/2,0,1m\neq-2,-1/2,0,1 admit exactly four local conservation laws: mass, energy (∫um+1/(m+1)​𝑑x\int u^{m+1}/(m+1)\,dx), and two trigonometric functionals. Her proof establishes that any conserved density depends at most on xx, tt, and uu (no derivatives), reducing the classification to a finite problem. A fifth conserved quantity (the nonlocal momentum I4I_{4} of Rosenau and Zilburg [17]) exists but falls outside the scope of local classification. Explicit forms of all five appear in Section 4.3. Vodová’s structural proof applies to all real m≠−2,−1/2,0,1m\neq-2,-1/2,0,1, not only integer exponents.

Integrable equations possess infinite conservation hierarchies generated by recursion operators. The abrupt termination at five laws, with no structural pattern suggesting continuation, provides direct evidence of non-integrability through conservation law counting.

(b) Absence of Lax pairs.

Systematic searches for differential operators LL and MM satisfying Lt=[M,L]L_{t}=[M,L] with K(m,m) dynamics find no valid candidates. The Hernández Heredero–Euler–Reyes classification [8] establishes through formal symmetry analysis that no recursion operator exists for K(m,m) with m>1m>1, which precludes the existence of Lax pairs. Applied to the K(m,m) family, the analysis shows that compatibility conditions for recursion operators fail at finite differential order. Each candidate either fails the compatibility condition or produces dynamics inconsistent with K(m,m). Without a Lax pair, the inverse scattering transform cannot be constructed, and the spectral theory that organizes integrable dynamics is unavailable.

(c) Painlevé test failure.

The Painlevé property requires that all movable singularities of solutions in the complex plane be poles. Dominant balance analysis of the K(m,m) traveling wave ODE reveals movable branch points for every m>1m>1: the leading singularity exponent −2/(m−1)-2/(m-1) is non-integer except at m=2m=2 and m=3m=3, and even those cases fail at higher-order resonance conditions. The detailed expansion is given in the Supplement, §S6.

(d) No bi-Hamiltonian structure.

K(m,m) equations admit a single Hamiltonian formulation through the third-order Poisson operator 𝔇=−(Dx3+Dx)\mathfrak{D}=-(D_{x}^{3}+D_{x}), with Dx=∂/∂xD_{x}=\partial/\partial x (Section 4.4). The bi-Hamiltonian criterion asks whether a compatible second Poisson operator exists, such that a recursion operator can be formed from the pair. Compatibility would generate the infinite conservation hierarchy through the Lenard recursion scheme [29, 12].

No such second operator exists. Vodová’s proof [46] that K(m,m) possesses no generalized symmetries of order greater than 33 implies that no recursion operator exists, which in turn precludes a compatible bi-Hamiltonian pair. The single Hamiltonian structure persists, but its extension to a compatible pair is impossible.

These four independent failures reinforce each other and the Hernández Heredero–Euler–Reyes classification. Among them, the classification theorem and the Painlevé analysis cover all real m>1m>1, while Vodová’s structural proof covers all real m≠−2,−1/2,0,1m\neq-2,-1/2,0,1 (Theorem 4.6). For integer exponents, all four arguments converge; for non-integer m∈(1,2)∪(2,∞)m\in(1,2)\cup(2,\infty), the classification and Painlevé test suffice to establish non-integrability independently.

The point is not that a Lax pair has merely not been found, or that no one has yet succeeded in extending the conservation hierarchy beyond five laws. The Hernández Heredero–Euler–Reyes classification proves, through finite-order obstruction arguments, that the required algebraic structures cannot exist for any real m>1m>1. K(m,m) non-integrability is a theorem, not a conjecture, and it holds throughout the compacton-bearing parameter range.

A reader familiar with the integrable paradigm of Section 2 now faces a clear question. K(m,m) compactons are elegant mathematical objects with explicit traveling wave solutions, systematic parameter relationships, and a finite but nontrivial conservation structure. Yet they are provably non-integrable: no Lax pairs, no inverse scattering, no infinite conservation hierarchy, no bi-Hamiltonian geometry. The standard theoretical apparatus is unavailable.

What mathematical structure, if any, remains?

4 Structure beyond integrability

Having established what K(m,m) compactons lack (§3), we turn to what they possess. The non-integrability results might suggest that little remains to say about these equations from an analytical perspective. The opposite is the case. Four subsections develop the evidence for systematic mathematical organization in the absence of complete integrability: universal algebraic formulas (§4.1), regularity classification (§4.2), finite conservation hierarchy (§4.3), and Hamiltonian geometry (§4.4). Detailed derivations supporting these topics are collected in Appendices E–G. The collision theory that converts these structural elements into dynamical predictions follows in §5.1.

4.1 Three universal formulas

Despite the non-integrability established in §3, the K(m,m) family harbors a striking regularity: three algebraic relationships connect every compacton’s shape, width, and speed to the single parameter mm. The K⁡(m,m)K(m,m) compacton was first derived in [15]; subsequent work verified individual cases and Rosenau and Zilburg [17] presented the general K(m,m) formula within their comprehensive summary of the 𝒞N​(m,a,b)\mathcal{C}_{N}(m,a,b) equation family, whose dispersion term 1b​[ua​(ub)x​x]x\frac{1}{b}[u^{a}(u^{b})_{xx}]_{x} reduces to that of K(m,n) at a=0a=0, b=nb=n (equation (2.35a) of that survey; see Appendix B). However, the existing treatments derive the formulas for specific values of mm or state the general result without a self-contained proof. The theorem below provides a unified derivation for all m>1m>1 simultaneously, extracts the structural mechanism behind each formula, and establishes consequences in Corollaries 4.2–4.4 and Proposition 5.3 (§5.1).

The compacton solutions take the form

U⁡(ξ)=A​cosα⁡(ξℓ),|ξ|≤π​ℓ2,U(\xi)=A\cos^{\alpha}\!\left(\frac{\xi}{\ell}\right),\qquad|\xi|\leq\frac{\pi\ell}{2}, (12)

with U⁡(ξ)=0U(\xi)=0 outside this interval. Here A>0A>0 is the amplitude, α\alpha governs the rate of approach to zero at the support boundary, and ℓ\ell controls the spatial width. The K(2,2) compacton was identified in [15], which also noted that expansion of the discrete chain with monomial average leads to K(m,m) compactons “of the form cos2/(m−1)\cos^{2/(m-1)}.” Rosenau [39] derived the 𝒞1​(2,1,1)\mathcal{C}_{1}(2,1,1) family explicitly. The 2018 survey [17] lists the general K(n,n) traveling compacton in equation (2.35a), expressed in the notation of the 𝒞N​(m,a,b)\mathcal{C}_{N}(m,a,b) framework.

The three relationships connecting the compacton parameters (α,ℓ,c)(\alpha,\ell,c) to the nonlinearity exponent mm, namely the edge exponent α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1), the width parameter ℓ=2​m/(m−1)\ell=2m/(m-1), and the speed–amplitude relation c=[(m+1)/(2​m)]​Am−1c=[(m+1)/(2m)]\,A^{m-1}, are implicit in the existing formula. The following theorem extracts all three simultaneously for arbitrary m>1m>1 and identifies the distinct mechanism behind each.

Theorem 4.1 (Universal Formulas for K(m,m) Compactons).

For m>1m>1, the K(m,m) equation

ut+(um)x+(um)x​x​x=0u_{t}+(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{m})_{xxx}=0 (8)

admits traveling wave solutions u⁡(x,t)=U⁡(x−c​t)u(x,t)=U(x-ct) of the form (12), where A>0A>0 is an arbitrary amplitude parameter and the three characteristic parameters are determined uniquely by mm:

α\displaystyle\alpha =2m−1\displaystyle=\frac{2}{m-1} (edge exponent), (13)
ℓ\displaystyle\ell =2​mm−1\displaystyle=\frac{2m}{m-1} (width parameter), (14)
c\displaystyle c =m+12​m​Am−1\displaystyle=\frac{m+1}{2m}\,A^{m-1} (speed–amplitude relation). (15)
Proof.

The argument extracts three independent constraints from the traveling wave ODE: with θ=ξ/ℓ\theta=\xi/\ell, matching the dominant powers of cos⁡θ\cos\theta determines α\alpha, balancing the coefficients of the leading power determines ℓ\ell, and the remaining balance determines cc.

Substituting u⁡(x,t)=U⁡(ξ)u(x,t)=U(\xi) with ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct into (8) and integrating once yields the traveling wave ODE

−c​U+Um+(Um)′′=0.-cU+U^{m}+(U^{m})^{\prime\prime}=0. (9)

The integration constant vanishes by requiring that both UU and the flux Um+(Um)′′U^{m}+(U^{m})^{\prime\prime} tend to zero at the support boundary |ξ|→π​ℓ/2|\xi|\to\pi\ell/2. For m≥4m\geq 4, the derivative U′U^{\prime} diverges at the support boundary (since α<1\alpha<1), but the product (Um)′=m​Um−1​U′(U^{m})^{\prime}=mU^{m-1}U^{\prime} remains bounded because the prefactor Um−1U^{m-1} decays fast enough to compensate. In particular, (Um)′∼(π/2−θ)m​α−1→0(U^{m})^{\prime}\sim(\pi/2-\theta)^{m\alpha-1}\to 0 as θ→π/2\theta\to\pi/2 whenever m​α>1m\alpha>1, which is satisfied for all m>1m>1 since m​α=2​m/(m−1)>2m\alpha=2m/(m-1)>2. The ODE is therefore analyzed on the open interval θ∈(−π/2,π/2)\theta\in(-\pi/2,\pi/2), where U>0U>0 and all terms are smooth.

Set θ=ξ/ℓ\theta=\xi/\ell so that d/d​ξ=ℓ−1​d/d​θd/d\xi=\ell^{-1}\,d/d\theta, and write U=A​cosα⁡θU=A\cos^{\alpha}\!\theta and Um=Am​cosγ⁡θU^{m}=A^{m}\cos^{\gamma}\!\theta, where γ=m​α\gamma=m\alpha. The second ξ\xi-derivative of UmU^{m} is (Um)′′=ℓ−2​(Um)θ​θ(U^{m})^{\prime\prime}=\ell^{-2}(U^{m})_{\theta\theta}. Computing (Am​cosγ⁡θ)θ​θ(A^{m}\cos^{\gamma}\!\theta)_{\theta\theta} by differentiating twice and applying sin2⁡θ=1−cos2⁡θ\sin^{2}\!\theta=1-\cos^{2}\!\theta gives

(Um)′′=Amℓ2​[γ⁡(γ−1)​cosγ−2⁡θ−γ2​cosγ⁡θ].(U^{m})^{\prime\prime}=\frac{A^{m}}{\ell^{2}}\Bigl[\gamma(\gamma-1)\cos^{\gamma-2}\!\theta-\gamma^{2}\cos^{\gamma}\!\theta\Bigr]. (16)

−c​A​cosα⁡θ+Am​cosγ⁡θ+Amℓ2​[γ⁡(γ−1)​cosγ−2⁡θ−γ2​cosγ⁡θ]=0.-cA\cos^{\alpha}\!\theta+A^{m}\cos^{\gamma}\!\theta+\frac{A^{m}}{\ell^{2}}\Bigl[\gamma(\gamma-1)\cos^{\gamma-2}\!\theta-\gamma^{2}\cos^{\gamma}\!\theta\Bigr]=0. (17)

This equation involves three powers of cos⁡θ\cos\theta: cosα⁡θ\cos^{\alpha}\!\theta, cosγ⁡θ\cos^{\gamma}\!\theta, and cosγ−2⁡θ\cos^{\gamma-2}\!\theta. For the equation to hold identically on (−π/2,π/2)(-\pi/2,\,\pi/2), coefficients of linearly independent powers must vanish separately. Since m>1m>1 implies γ>α\gamma>\alpha, the power cosα⁡θ\cos^{\alpha}\!\theta is independent of cosγ⁡θ\cos^{\gamma}\!\theta. The term −c​U=−c​A​cosα⁡θ-cU=-cA\cos^{\alpha}\!\theta can balance with the cosγ−2⁡θ\cos^{\gamma-2}\!\theta term from the dispersion only if α=γ−2=m​α−2\alpha=\gamma-2=m\alpha-2. Solving:

α⁡(1−m)=−2⟹α=2m−1,\alpha(1-m)=-2\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\alpha=\frac{2}{m-1},

Am​[1−γ2ℓ2]=0⟹ℓ=γ=2​mm−1,A^{m}\Bigl[1-\frac{\gamma^{2}}{\ell^{2}}\Bigr]=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad\ell=\gamma=\frac{2m}{m-1},

−c​A+Amℓ2​γ​(γ−1)=0⟹c=Am−1​γ−1γ=m+12​m​Am−1,-cA+\frac{A^{m}}{\ell^{2}}\,\gamma(\gamma-1)=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad c=A^{m-1}\,\frac{\gamma-1}{\gamma}=\frac{m+1}{2m}\,A^{m-1},
