At the support boundary θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2, the solution satisfies U⁡(ξ0)=0U(\xi_{0})=0 and the flux condition (Um)′​(ξ0−)=0(U^{m})^{\prime}(\xi_{0}^{-})=0, matching the exterior solution U≡0U\equiv 0. ∎

Each formula in Theorem 4.1 has a distinct structural origin. Power matching determines the edge exponent: α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1) is the unique value for which the translation term −c​U-cU and the dispersive term (Um)′′(U^{m})^{\prime\prime} contribute to the same power of cos⁡θ\cos\theta. Coefficient cancellation determines the width: forcing the nonlinear term UmU^{m} and the leading part of the dispersion to cancel at order cosγ⁡θ\cos^{\gamma}\!\theta requires ℓ=γ=2​m/(m−1)\ell=\gamma=2m/(m-1). Finally, amplitude–speed balance determines the propagation speed: the remaining terms at order cosγ−2⁡θ\cos^{\gamma-2}\!\theta yield c=[(m+1)/(2​m)]​Am−1c=[(m+1)/(2m)]\,A^{m-1}. Together, these constraints exhaust the information available from the cosine-power ansatz.

Verification and immediate consequences

Supplement Table S1 confirms the theorem across m=2m=2 through m=7m=7, including the limiting behavior as m→∞m\to\infty.

Several consequences follow directly from the universal formulas.

Corollary 4.2 (Width Independence).

The compacton support width W=π​ℓ=2​π​m/(m−1)W=\pi\ell=2\pi m/(m-1) depends only on mm and is independent of amplitude AA.

This property has no analog for KdV solitons, whose width scales as A−1/2A^{-1/2}. A tall K(m,m) compacton and a short one occupy the same spatial extent; they travel at different speeds but maintain identical profiles up to vertical rescaling.

Corollary 4.3 (Product Identity).

The edge exponent and width parameter satisfy

α⋅ℓ=4​m(m−1)2,\alpha\cdot\ell=\frac{4m}{(m-1)^{2}}, (18)

connecting boundary regularity to spatial extent through a single algebraic relation.

This product decreases monotonically from 88 at m=2m=2 toward 00 as m→∞m\to\infty. Since α\alpha governs boundary regularity and ℓ\ell governs width, sharper edges necessarily accompany narrower supports within the K(m,m) family.

Corollary 4.4 (Speed Coefficient Bounds).

The speed coefficient k⁡(m)=(m+1)/(2​m)k(m)=(m+1)/(2m) decreases monotonically from k⁡(2)=3/4k(2)=3/4 toward k⁡(∞)=1/2k(\infty)=1/2 as m→∞m\to\infty.

Higher nonlinearity reduces the speed gained per unit amplitude increase. In the limit m→∞m\to\infty, the speed–amplitude relation approaches c=Am−1/2c=A^{m-1}/2, where the growing exponent compensates for the halved coefficient.

Corollary 4.5 (Monotonicity along the compacton family).

For all m>1m>1 and A>0A>0, the speed–amplitude relation satisfies d​c/d​A>0dc/dA>0:

d​cd​A=(m+1)​(m−1)2​m​Am−2>0.\frac{dc}{dA}=\frac{(m+1)(m-1)}{2m}\,A^{m-2}>0. (19)

Equivalently, the mass I0=Cm​AI_{0}=C_{m}A, with Cm=ℓ​B​(α+12,12)C_{m}=\ell\,B\bigl(\frac{\alpha+1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\bigr) from (63), and the translation generator P=12​I4=(m+1)​I1/(2​c)P=\tfrac{1}{2}I_{4}=(m+1)\,I_{1}/(2c), which is proportional to c2/(m−1)c^{2/(m-1)}, are strictly increasing functions of cc.

The expression for PP follows from (Dx2+1)​Um=c​U(D_{x}^{2}+1)U^{m}=cU, which gives (Dx2+1)−1​U=Um/c(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1}U=U^{m}/c. The slope condition of Vakhitov and Kolokolov [45] and of the Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss framework [6] concerns d​P/d​cdP/dc, the derivative of the conserved quantity that generates the symmetry, here translation; the mass I0I_{0} is a Casimir and does not enter it. Even with PP the framework yields no stability conclusion for K(m,m). Because ℋ\mathcal{H} has no quadratic part, the second variation of ℋ−c​P\mathcal{H}-cP at a compacton reduces to −c​(Dx2+1)−1-c\,(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1} on perturbations supported away from it, and is negative on slowly varying ones, so it has infinitely many negative directions where the theory requires one. Stability of compactons therefore remains open (Problem 3 of Appendix K).

Structural contrast with integrable systems

In the absence of spectral theory, the universal formulas establish an organizing principle different from, but comparable in kind to, the inverse scattering transform for KdV. For integrable equations, the IST yields exact multi-soliton formulas from spectral data: soliton parameters are encoded in discrete eigenvalues and norming constants of the Lax operator [24, 1]. For K(m,m), no spectral theory exists: there are no Lax pairs, no recursion operators, no scattering data. What remains is scaling universality: three closed-form relationships predicting all compacton properties from the single parameter mm. The methods are different, the machinery is different, but the output is the same kind of mathematical knowledge: algebraic formulas that govern a family of nonlinear wave solutions.

A notable structural consequence is the identity ℓ−α=2\ell-\alpha=2, which holds for all m>1m>1. This identity implies that the trigonometric conservation integrals ∫U​sin⁡(x)​𝑑x\int U\sin(x)\,dx and ∫U​cos⁡(x)​𝑑x\int U\cos(x)\,dx vanish identically for every K(m,m) compacton, a property noted empirically for K⁡(2,2)K(2,2) in [15] and proved in full generality in Proposition 5.3 and Appendix A. This vanishing has significant consequences for the collision constraint analysis in §5.1.

The proof makes no use of mm being an integer. For any real m>1m>1, the formulas (13)–(15) define a compacton profile that formally satisfies the traveling wave ODE. We emphasize that Theorem 4.1 establishes the existence of cosine-power compactons; the question of whether other compact-support traveling waves exist with different profiles remains open (Problem 1 in Appendix K). The continuous dependence on mm opens the possibility of studying K(m,m) equations along continuous paths in parameter space, with regularity transitions occurring at m=3m=3 (where α\alpha crosses unity) serving as a codimension-one bifurcation. The regularity classification that follows from Theorem 4.1 is developed in the next subsection.

4.2 Regularity classification

The edge exponent α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1) governs more than the rate of approach to zero. It determines the entire regularity landscape of K(m,m) compactons, classifying each member of the family into one of three qualitatively distinct regimes. This classification follows directly from Theorem 4.1: once α\alpha is known as a function of mm, the regularity character at the support boundary is determined by comparing α\alpha with unity.

Three regularity regimes

Near the support boundary ξ0=π​ℓ/2\xi_{0}=\pi\ell/2, the compacton profile satisfies U⁡(ξ)∼B​(ξ0−ξ)αU(\xi)\sim B(\xi_{0}-\xi)^{\alpha} with derivative U′​(ξ)∼−α​B​(ξ0−ξ)α−1U^{\prime}(\xi)\sim-\alpha B(\xi_{0}-\xi)^{\alpha-1}, so the classification reduces to the sign of α−1\alpha-1. For m<3m<3 (α>1\alpha>1), the derivative vanishes at the boundary and the compacton is at least C1C^{1}; the traveling wave ODE (9) holds pointwise. At m=3m=3 (α=1\alpha=1), the derivative reaches a nonzero limit, producing a cusp where U′U^{\prime} jumps discontinuously; K(3,3) with U⁡(ξ)=A​cos⁡(ξ/3)U(\xi)=A\cos(\xi/3) is the canonical example. For m>3m>3 (α<1\alpha<1), the derivative diverges:

U′​(ξ)∼−α​B​(ξ0−ξ)α−1→−∞as ​ξ→ξ0−.U^{\prime}(\xi)\sim-\alpha B(\xi_{0}-\xi)^{\alpha-1}\to-\infty\quad\text{as }\xi\to\xi_{0}^{-}. (20)

Solutions in this regime belong to C0,αC^{0,\alpha} (Hölder continuous with exponent α\alpha) but not to C1C^{1}, and a weak formulation becomes necessary [17]. Table 1 catalogs the classification across the family.

The cusp transition as a codimension-one event

As mm increases through 33, the edge exponent α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1) crosses unity and the qualitative character of boundary regularity changes: the derivative transitions from vanishing (m<3m<3) through a finite jump (m=3m=3) to divergence (m>3m>3). This is a codimension-one event in parameter space. The transition has analytical significance: in variational stability theory [6, 7], regularity at solitary wave boundaries determines the function spaces in which an analysis can be posed, and the cusp at m=3m=3 is exactly the point where this determination changes for K(m,m).

Weak solutions and distributional formulation

For m>3m>3, the classical strong form of the traveling wave ODE breaks down at the support boundary where U′U^{\prime} diverges. A weak (distributional) formulation replaces pointwise validity with integral conditions: a bounded measurable function uu is a weak solution if

∫0T∫ℝ[u​φt+um​φx+um​φx​x​x]​𝑑x​𝑑t=0\int_{0}^{T}\!\!\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl[u\,\varphi_{t}+u^{m}\,\varphi_{x}+u^{m}\,\varphi_{xxx}\bigr]\,dx\,dt=0 (21)

for all test functions φ∈Cc∞​(ℝ×(0,T))\varphi\in C_{c}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}\times(0,T)). All five conservation laws extend to this weak setting, a fact essential for the constraint analysis in §5.1; the detailed argument appears in Appendix E.

Limiting behavior and connections

As m→∞m\to\infty, the edge exponent α→0+\alpha\to 0^{+} and the support width W=π​ℓ→2​πW=\pi\ell\to 2\pi. The compacton profile approaches a limiting shape square-wave pulse. The K(m,m) family provides a one-parameter path from smooth K(2,2) compactons through the cusp at K(3,3) toward square-wave-like structures, with regularity degrading monotonically along this path. Whether the m→∞m\to\infty limit yields a well-defined singular solution, which remains an open question (Appendix K).

4.3 Finite conservation laws

Integrable equations carry infinite hierarchies of conservation laws, generated through recursion operators from bi-Hamiltonian structure [29, 12]. These hierarchies encode the algebraic backbone of integrability: each new conservation law constrains the dynamics further, and taken together they determine the solution completely. What happens when that hierarchy terminates?

For K(m,m) equations, Vodová [46] answered this question through an exhaustive computational classification.

Theorem 4.6 (Finite Conservation Hierarchy [46]).

For m≠−2,−1/2,0,1m\neq-2,-1/2,0,1, the K(m,m) equation (8) admits exactly four functionally independent local conservation laws. In addition, one nonlocal conservation law exists [17], bringing the known count of independent conserved quantities to five. Whether additional nonlocal laws exist remains open (see the discussion following this theorem).

Vodová’s proof [46] is structural rather than computational. The K(m,m) equation is Hamiltonian with respect to the third-order Poisson operator 𝔇=−(Dx3+Dx)\mathfrak{D}=-(D_{x}^{3}+D_{x}) (see §4.4). Any conserved density ρ\rho yields a cosymmetry γ=δ​ρ/δ​u\gamma=\delta\rho/\delta u, and 𝔇\mathfrak{D} maps cosymmetries to symmetries. Vodová first establishes (Proposition 2 in [46]) that no generalized symmetries of order greater than 33 exist. If γ\gamma had differential order K>0K>0, then 𝔇⁡(γ)\mathfrak{D}(\gamma) would be a symmetry of order 3+K>33+K>3, contradicting the symmetry bound. Therefore every cosymmetry depends at most on xx, tt, and uu, and consequently every conserved density ρ\rho depends at most on xx, tt, and uu. Enumerating such densities is then a finite problem, yielding exactly four solutions.

The fifth conserved quantity is the nonlocal functional I4I_{4} defined in (26) below, whose density involves the integral operator (Dx2+1)−1(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1} and therefore falls outside the scope of Vodová’s local classification. Independence from I0I_{0}–I3I_{3} follows because I4I_{4} is a nonlocal bilinear functional of uu, whereas each local law has a density depending on uu alone (pointwise in xx). Its conservation follows from the factorization 𝔇=−Dx​(Dx2+1)\mathfrak{D}=-D_{x}(D_{x}^{2}+1); the proof is given below. Vodová’s argument establishes maximality for local conservation laws through a rigorous symmetry-order bound, but the question of whether additional nonlocal conserved quantities exist beyond I4I_{4} remains open; a formal impossibility proof for higher-order nonlocal densities has not been obtained.

Remark 4.7 (Distributional framework).

Anco and Gandarias [2] subsequently developed a rigorous distributional framework for these conservation laws, showing that weak compacton solutions satisfy the associated continuity equations in a well-defined distributional sense even at the support boundary where classical derivatives may not exist. This framework places the formal conservation law identities on firm analytical footing for the class of compacton solutions with finite regularity at the support edges.

The five conservation laws

Four of the five laws are local; the fifth is nonlocal, coupling distant spatial points through an integral operator. Full derivations appear in Appendix F.

Mass.
I0=∫−∞∞u​𝑑x.I_{0}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u\,dx. (22)

Mass conservation follows directly from the divergence structure of K(m,m); in the Hamiltonian formulation of §4.4 it is a Casimir of 𝔇\mathfrak{D} (a functional whose variational derivative lies in the kernel of 𝔇\mathfrak{D}, so that it is conserved by every flow of the form ut=𝔇⁡(f)u_{t}=\mathfrak{D}(f)), while spatial translation invariance corresponds through Noether’s theorem to the nonlocal momentum I4I_{4} [35, 13, 17].

Energy.
I1=∫−∞∞um+1m+1​𝑑x.I_{1}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{u^{m+1}}{m+1}\,dx. (23)

Energy is the Hamiltonian for the K(m,m) evolution (§4.4), associated with time-translation invariance through Noether’s theorem.

Trigonometric laws.
I2\displaystyle I_{2} =∫−∞∞u​sin⁡(x)​𝑑x,\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u\sin(x)\,dx, (24)
I3\displaystyle I_{3} =∫−∞∞u​cos⁡(x)​𝑑x.\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u\cos(x)\,dx. (25)

These project the solution onto its fundamental Fourier mode at wavenumber k=1k=1: the complex combination I3−i​I2=u^​(1,t)I_{3}-iI_{2}=\hat{u}(1,t), where u^​(k,t)=∫u​e−i​k​x​𝑑x\hat{u}(k,t)=\int u\,e^{-ikx}\,dx. Conservation follows from exact cancellation between the convection and dispersion terms at this specific wavenumber (Appendix F). No higher Fourier modes yield conservation laws.

Nonlocal momentum.
I4=∫−∞∞u⁡(x)​(Dx2+1)−1​[u]​(x)​𝑑x,I_{4}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}u(x)\,(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1}[u](x)\,dx, (26)

where (Dx2+1)−1(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1} denotes the pseudoinverse of Dx2+1D_{x}^{2}+1: on the Fourier side, it acts as the multiplier 1/(1−k2)1/(1-k^{2}), which is well-defined on functions satisfying u^​(±1)=0\hat{u}(\pm 1)=0, precisely the condition guaranteed by conservation of I2I_{2} and I3I_{3} for compacton solutions. Rosenau and Zilburg [17, Lemma 1] obtained I4I_{4} from a Lagrangian formulation of K(n,n), as the momentum associated with translation invariance. It falls outside Vodová’s local classification and instead arises from the factorization of the Hamiltonian operator 𝔇=−Dx​(Dx2+1)\mathfrak{D}=-D_{x}(D_{x}^{2}+1). Conservation of I4I_{4} requires m=nm=n and thus reflects the specific algebraic structure of K(m,m); the proof is given in Appendix F.

Structural contrast with integrable hierarchies

A direct comparison highlights what the finite hierarchy means (Table 2).

In KdV, the recursion operator ℛ=𝒥2​𝒥1−1\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{J}_{2}\mathcal{J}_{1}^{-1} generates conservation laws indefinitely. Given the nn-th conserved density, applying ℛ\mathcal{R} produces the (n+1)(n+1)-st. The resulting infinite family is in involution: all Poisson brackets {Ij,Ik}\{I_{j},I_{k}\} vanish, providing the complete integrability in the sense of Liouville [3]. The inverse scattering transform [13, 24] translates this algebraic structure into explicit multi-soliton solutions.

For K(m,m), no recursion operator exists (Theorem 3.1), and the hierarchy terminates. Theorem 4.6 quantifies the termination. The five known laws are in involution under the Poisson bracket (30) of §4.4: three are Casimirs, and, with ℋ=I1\mathcal{H}=I_{1} the Hamiltonian (27), {ℋ,I4}=−2∫umuxdx=0\{\mathcal{H},I_{4}\}=-2\int u^{m}u_{x}\,dx=0. The two non-Casimir functionals generate the K(m,m) time flow, Xℋ=𝔇​δ​ℋ/δ​uX_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathfrak{D}\,\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta u, and spatial translation, XP=−uxX_{P}=-u_{x} for P=12​I4P=\tfrac{1}{2}I_{4}; these commute, and a traveling wave is the relative equilibrium on which Xℋ=c​XPX_{\mathcal{H}}=c\,X_{P}. Beyond this pair the known laws furnish no further independent commuting flows. That shortage, not any failure of the laws to commute, marks non-integrability.

Origin and structure of the five laws

The Hamiltonian operator 𝔇=−(Dx3+Dx)\mathfrak{D}=-(D_{x}^{3}+D_{x}) accounts for all five known conservation laws through its algebraic structure. Its formal kernel ker⁡(𝔇)\ker(\mathfrak{D}), spanned by {1,cos⁡x,sin⁡x}\{1,\cos x,\sin x\}, generates three Casimir functionals: mass I0I_{0} and the trigonometric pair I2I_{2}, I3I_{3}. (Although {1,cos⁡x,sin⁡x}∉L2​(ℝ)\{1,\cos x,\sin x\}\notin L^{2}(\mathbb{R}), their action as Casimir densities is rigorously defined through the L2L^{2} duality pairing with compacton solutions in Lc1​(ℝ)L^{1}_{c}(\mathbb{R}), the integrable functions of compact support.) These are conserved for any evolution of the form ut=𝔇⁡(f)u_{t}=\mathfrak{D}(f), regardless of the choice of ff. The fourth local law I1I_{1} (energy) is the Hamiltonian itself, and the nonlocal I4I_{4} arises from the factorization 𝔇=−Dx​(Dx2+1)\mathfrak{D}=-D_{x}(D_{x}^{2}+1). The detailed Casimir analysis and evaluated conservation integrals for individual compactons appear in Appendix F.

These five quantities provide the known conservation constraints governing K(m,m) dynamics. Their role in controlling collision outcomes is the subject of §5.1.

4.4 Hamiltonian geometry without bi-Hamiltonian structure

The K(m,m) equation arises naturally as a Hamiltonian system. Rosenau and Zilburg [17, §7.1] gave Hamiltonian and Lagrangian formulations of the K(n,n) and K(n+1,n) equations; the formulation below follows theirs for K(n,n). Define the functional

ℋ⁡[u]=∫−∞∞um+1m+1​𝑑x,\mathcal{H}[u]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{u^{m+1}}{m+1}\,dx, (27)

and the third-order Poisson operator

𝔇=−(Dx3+Dx).\mathfrak{D}=-(D_{x}^{3}+D_{x}). (28)

The K(m,m) equation (8) is then equivalent to

ut=𝔇​δ​ℋδ​u,u_{t}=\mathfrak{D}\,\frac{\delta\mathcal{H}}{\delta u}, (29)

since δ​ℋ/δ​u=um\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta u=u^{m} and 𝔇⁡(um)=−(um)x​x​x−(um)x\mathfrak{D}(u^{m})=-(u^{m})_{xxx}-(u^{m})_{x}. The operator 𝔇\mathfrak{D} is skew-adjoint and satisfies the Jacobi identity, making it a valid Poisson operator [13, 46]. The Hamiltonian ℋ\mathcal{H} is itself conserved: the antisymmetry of 𝔇\mathfrak{D} ensures d​ℋ/d​t=⟨δ​ℋ/δ​u,𝔇​δ​ℋ/δ​u⟩=0d\mathcal{H}/dt=\langle\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta u,\,\mathfrak{D}\,\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta u\rangle=0. This identifies ℋ\mathcal{H} with the energy conservation law I1I_{1} of §4.3.

This formulation induces a Poisson bracket on the space of functionals:

{F,G}=∫δ​Fδ​u​𝔇​[δ​Gδ​u]​𝑑x,\{F,G\}=\int\frac{\delta F}{\delta u}\,\mathfrak{D}\!\left[\frac{\delta G}{\delta u}\right]dx, (30)

satisfying antisymmetry, bilinearity, and the Jacobi identity. Any functional with {F,ℋ}=0\{F,\mathcal{H}\}=0 is conserved. The five conservation laws from Theorem 4.6 all satisfy this condition, and the bracket provides a unified algebraic framework relating them.

A notable feature of the K(m,m) Hamiltonian structure is the factorization 𝔇=−Dx​(Dx2+1)\mathfrak{D}=-D_{x}(D_{x}^{2}+1), whose three-dimensional kernel generates the three Casimirs; the origin of each conservation law is traced in §4.3.

The bi-Hamiltonian obstruction

KdV possesses two compatible Hamiltonian structures whose recursion operator ℛ=𝒥2​𝒥1−1\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{J}_{2}\,\mathcal{J}_{1}^{-1} generates the infinite conservation hierarchy through the Lenard scheme [29, 12]. Compact support does not by itself rule out such a pair: Olver and Rosenau [38] built integrable bi-Hamiltonian equations with compacton solutions from compatible Hamiltonian triples. K(m,m) admits no such extension. Systematic searches for a second Poisson operator compatible with 𝔇\mathfrak{D} fail for all m≥2m\geq 2, a consequence of Vodová’s proof that no generalized symmetries of order greater than 33 exist [46]: a compatible second operator would induce such symmetries through recursion. The nonlinear dispersion (um)x​x​x(u^{m})_{xxx} is the root cause.

Without the compatible pair, three consequences follow: no recursion operator operates (explaining the hierarchy termination), the conserved functionals, though in involution, generate only two commuting flows, time evolution and translation (three are Casimirs), and the reduction to action-angle variables is unavailable [3]. The detailed obstruction analysis appears in Appendix G.

What persists from the integrable world

Despite the failure of bi-Hamiltonian structure, K(m,m) retains substantial geometric machinery from the Hamiltonian framework.

Variational principles. The traveling wave solutions of Theorem 4.1 arise from the Hamiltonian structure. Substituting the traveling-wave ansatz u⁡(x,t)=U⁡(x−c​t)u(x,t)=U(x-ct) into ut=𝔇⁡(δ​ℋ/δ​u)u_{t}=\mathfrak{D}(\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta u) and integrating once yields (Dx2+1)​(Um)=c​U(D_{x}^{2}+1)(U^{m})=cU, the traveling wave ODE whose phase-plane analysis is developed in §7.

Stability theory. The standard route to orbital stability uses ℋ−c​P\mathcal{H}-cP as a Lyapunov functional and examines its second variation at the traveling wave [4, 6]. For K(m,m) this route is blocked for every m>1m>1: the second variation has infinitely many negative directions (see the remark after Corollary 4.5).

Conservation law origins. Each of the five laws has a geometric origin in 𝔇\mathfrak{D} (§4.3), and the local hierarchy is finite, reflecting the finite-dimensional symmetry algebra established by Vodová [46].

The situation can be summarized concisely. K(m,m) is Hamiltonian but not bi-Hamiltonian. It possesses a Poisson structure (sufficient for constructing structure-preserving numerical integrators), variational principles, and a Noether correspondence, but lacks the recursion mechanism that converts these ingredients into complete integrability. The five conservation laws constrain the dynamics strongly but not completely. The gap between strong constraint and complete determination manifests as quasi-elastic collision behavior: emerging compactons retain most of their pre-collision identities, while small but nonzero debris fields absorb the remaining degrees of freedom (§5.1).

Variational characterization of traveling waves.

Formally, for perturbations in the domain of (Dx2+1)−1(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1} (§4.3), set P:=12​I4P:=\tfrac{1}{2}I_{4}, so that δ​P/δ​u=(Dx2+1)−1​u\delta P/\delta u=(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1}u and 𝔇​δ​P/δ​u=−ux\mathfrak{D}\,\delta P/\delta u=-u_{x}: PP generates translations. For a traveling wave u=U⁡(x−c​t)u=U(x-ct) one has ut=−c​U′=𝔇​δ​ℋ/δ​u=c​𝔇​δ​P/δ​uu_{t}=-cU^{\prime}=\mathfrak{D}\,\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta u=c\,\mathfrak{D}\,\delta P/\delta u, hence

δ​ℋδ​u=c​δ​Pδ​u+κ,κ∈ker⁡𝔇=span⁡{1,cos⁡x,sin⁡x}.\frac{\delta\mathcal{H}}{\delta u}=c\,\frac{\delta P}{\delta u}+\kappa,\qquad\kappa\in\ker\mathfrak{D}=\operatorname{span}\{1,\cos x,\sin x\}.

Applying (Dx2+1)(D_{x}^{2}+1) recovers the once-integrated traveling-wave ODE −c​U+Um+(Um)′′=C0-cU+U^{m}+(U^{m})^{\prime\prime}=C_{0}, with the integration constant C0C_{0} equal to the constant Casimir component of κ\kappa; (9) is the case C0=0C_{0}=0, and (34) is its form on a positive background u=au=a (§7), for which ℋ\mathcal{H} and PP are renormalized by subtracting their values at u≡au\equiv a and varied with respect to f=U−af=U-a.

5 Collision dynamics and the constraint-deficit mechanism

The universal formulas, conservation hierarchy, and Hamiltonian geometry of the preceding section describe the static structure of K(m,m) compactons. This section turns to dynamics: what happens when compactons collide? The constraint-deficit mechanism (Theorem 5.1) provides a precise answer, and comparison with solitary waves of the Benjamin–Bona–Mahony (BBM) equation [5] (§5.2) reveals that interaction geometry plays an independent role alongside conservation law count. A concluding subsection positions the constraint-deficit framework as a potential tool for analyzing near-integrability in other dispersive PDEs.

5.1 Quasi-elastic collisions and the constraint-deficit mechanism

Two K(m,m) compactons with amplitudes A1>A2>0A_{1}>A_{2}>0 and speeds c1>c2c_{1}>c_{2} will eventually collide when the faster wave overtakes the slower (Figure 3). The post-collision state consists of two principal compactons with amplitudes A1′,A2′A^{\prime}_{1},A^{\prime}_{2} (primes mark post-collision values), asymptotic phase shifts δ1,δ2\delta_{1},\delta_{2} (Figure 3(d)), and a residual debris field w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) of small amplitude spreading dispersively behind the emergent waves [15, 17]. The numerically resolved debris w=u−ucompactonsw=u-u_{\mathrm{compactons}} is continuous on the periodic computational domain, hence bounded and square-integrable, ensuring that its Fourier analysis is well-defined.

Numerical simulations reveal a consistent pattern across the K(m,m) family (Figure 3): the principal compactons emerge with amplitudes close to their pre-collision values, while the debris field carries a small fraction of the total energy [15, 22]. To quantify this, define the elasticity coefficient

ℰ=A1′+A2′A1+A2,\mathcal{E}=\frac{A^{\prime}_{1}+A^{\prime}_{2}}{A_{1}+A_{2}}, (31)

measuring the fraction of total amplitude retained by the principal waves. For K(2,2) with A1=1.0A_{1}=1.0, A2=0.8A_{2}=0.8, our simulations (pseudospectral method (PSM), Nx=512N_{x}=512 grid points, domain [0,200][0,200], dissipation coefficient δ=0.15\delta=0.15) with the principal waves recovered by least-squares fit of the exact profile, give A1′≈1.0008A^{\prime}_{1}\approx 1.0008, A2′≈0.7987A^{\prime}_{2}\approx 0.7987, yielding ℰ≈0.9997\mathcal{E}\approx 0.9997; these values are unchanged at Nx=1024N_{x}=1024. The debris field ww carries approximately 0.03%0.03\% of the squared L2L^{2} norm ∫u2​𝑑x\int u^{2}\,dx; the principal waves retain all but 6×10−56\times 10^{-5} of their Hamiltonian energy according to the fitted amplitudes; at the 10−410^{-4} precision of the fit this is an upper bound on the true deficit.

Alternative elasticity measures.

Several natural alternatives to (31) exist, including energy-based and L2L^{2}-based measures. For K(m,m) compactons, all standard measures are related by monotone transformations of the amplitude ratio, so the within-family ordering is invariant under the choice of measure; see Appendix H for the detailed comparison.

These values are consistent with earlier simulations [15, 22]. For K(3,3) with A1=1.5A_{1}=1.5, A2=1.0A_{2}=1.0, the same method gives A1′≈1.5001A^{\prime}_{1}\approx 1.5001, A2′≈0.9990A^{\prime}_{2}\approx 0.9990 and ℰ≈0.9996\mathcal{E}\approx 0.9996, with debris again near 0.03%0.03\% of the squared L2L^{2} norm and a fitted-amplitude Hamiltonian deficit of at most 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}, again limited by the fit precision. Recent high-resolution simulations by Garralón-López, Rus, and Villatoro [14] have extended these observations to compacton-anticompacton collisions, where the interaction geometry is more violent. Their results reveal a striking odd-even asymmetry in the nonlinearity exponent, which they denote pp (our mm): for odd pp (= 3, 5, 7), collisions remain robust even with minimal hyperviscosity regularization, while even pp (= 2, 4, 6) produces blow-up unless the amplitude ratio lies below a threshold. The same group established that the absolute-value variant |K|​(p,p)|K|(p,p) admits compactons for non-integer pp, extending the parameter space beyond the integer cases treated here [5], and developed an adiabatic perturbation theory quantifying how hyperviscosity affects compacton evolution [16]. These numerical findings complement and extend the analytical framework below.

Numerical method.

The compact support of K(m,n)(m,n) compactons poses challenges for standard spectral methods, which suffer from Gibbs oscillations at the support boundary. We employ a spectrally-filtered pseudospectral method that combines joint low-pass filtering of both nonlinear flux terms (Variant C, with cutoff wavenumber kmax/qk_{\max}/q and q=2q=2) with a biharmonic high-pass dissipation operator concentrated near the compacton boundary by a smooth spatial ramp. The dissipation coefficient δ=0.15\delta=0.15, scaled by the instantaneous maximum wave speed cmax=m+12​m​max⁡|u|m−1c_{\max}=\tfrac{m+1}{2m}\max|u|^{m-1}, is universal across all values of mm tested. Full details, including the boundary-layer analysis motivating the cmaxc_{\max} scaling, are given in Appendix D and in [9]. Code implementing these simulations is available at https://github.com/machyman/kmm-compactons.

These collisions are neither perfectly elastic nor strongly inelastic. The question is why.

A shift of perspective.

Peter Lax spent much of his career analyzing approaches to eliminate numerical oscillations behind steep fronts, a recurring challenge in the numerical approximation of shock waves. Late in his career, he shifted focus to understanding these oscillations and, with Dave Levermore, developed the theory of the zero-dispersion limit of the KdV equation [28], revealing that the oscillations encode deep information about the underlying dispersive structure. In the same spirit, after spending much of my career focused on elastic soliton collisions, I now turn to analyzing the small but persistent inelasticity of compacton collisions. The constraint-deficit mechanism (Theorem 5.1) provides a concrete, quantitative explanation for why these collisions are near-elastic but not perfectly so, and what the residual debris reveals about the gap between finite and infinite conservation hierarchies.

Why collisions cannot be perfectly elastic

Three hypotheses underlie the analysis below. All are supported by available numerical evidence but have not yet been proved rigorously. We state them explicitly so that the logical dependence of the subsequent results is transparent.

  1. (H1)

    Two-compacton emergence. After a binary collision, the post-collision state consists of exactly two principal compactons plus a dispersive debris field of small amplitude. This behavior has been observed in extensive numerical studies spanning three decades, including Rosenau–Hyman [15], Ismail–Taha [22], Cooper–Mihaila–Saxena [8, 31], and Garralón–Rus–Villatoro [14, 16]. No simulation has produced a third compacton or a non-compacton localized structure; the recent high-resolution studies [14, 16] tracked collision dynamics over thousands of time units with no deviation from this pattern.

  2. (H2)

    Profile preservation. The emergent compactons take the cosine-power form established in Theorem 4.1, with possibly modified amplitudes and phase shifts. This hypothesis follows from Proposition B.2: within the class of positive, symmetric, single-hump traveling waves with compact support, the cosine-power profile is the unique solution of the traveling wave ODE. The only additional assumption is that emergent localized structures are positive and symmetric, a property observed in all reported numerical simulations.

  3. (H3)

    Conservation law completeness. The four local conservation laws classified by Vodová [46] together with the nonlocal functional I4I_{4} exhaust the independent conserved quantities. Vodová’s structural proof establishes local completeness rigorously for all real m≠−2,−1/2,0,1m\neq-2,-1/2,0,1; the assumption here is that no additional nonlocal conserved quantities exist beyond I4I_{4}.

Under these hypotheses, the answer to why collisions are not perfectly elastic lies in the constraint structure of the five conservation laws. The following theorem, conditional on hypotheses (H1)–(H3) above, shows that perfect elasticity imposes incompatible demands.

Theorem 5.1 (Constraint deficit (assuming H1–H3)).

For a two-compacton collision in K(m,m), m≥2m\geq 2:

  1. (a)

    The post-collision debris field w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) has infinitely many degrees of freedom, parameterized by its Fourier spectrum {w^​(k)}k∈ℝ\{\hat{w}(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{R}}.

  2. (b)

    The five conservation laws impose five scalar constraints on the post-collision state. Two of these (mass I0I_{0} and energy I1I_{1}) constrain the emergent compacton amplitudes: given the debris mass MwM_{w} and energy EwE_{w}, they locally determine (A1′,A2′)(A^{\prime}_{1},A^{\prime}_{2}) near (A1,A2)(A_{1},A_{2}) by the implicit function theorem. Two (the trigonometric laws I2I_{2}, I3I_{3}) constrain the fundamental Fourier mode of the debris field; and one (I4I_{4}) couples the debris to the compacton configuration.

  3. (c)

    In an integrable system, the infinite conservation hierarchy constrains every radiation mode, forcing zero debris. In K(m,m), the five laws leave all debris Fourier modes w^​(k)\hat{w}(k) with k≠1k\neq 1 unconstrained. This gap between finitely many radiation constraints and infinitely many radiation degrees of freedom is the mechanism by which K(m,m) collisions generate debris. Whether this mechanism extends to other non-integrable dispersive systems remains to be established.

Argument assuming H1–H3.

Part (a): By Theorem 4.1, each post-collision compacton is determined by a single amplitude parameter Ai′A^{\prime}_{i} and a phase shift δi\delta_{i}. The debris field w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) adds infinitely many degrees of freedom through its Fourier spectrum.

Part (b): The five conservation laws (22)–(26) provide five independent scalar equations relating pre- and post-collision quantities. We partition these by what they constrain.

Amplitude constraints. Mass conservation gives Cm​(A1′+A2′)+Mw=Cm​(A1+A2)C_{m}(A^{\prime}_{1}+A^{\prime}_{2})+M_{w}=C_{m}(A_{1}+A_{2}) and energy conservation gives Dm​(A1′m+1+A2′m+1)+Ew=Dm​(A1m+1+A2m+1)D_{m}(A^{\prime\,m+1}_{1}+A^{\prime\,m+1}_{2})+E_{w}=D_{m}(A_{1}^{m+1}+A_{2}^{m+1}), where Cm,DmC_{m},D_{m} are the mass and energy integral coefficients of (63)–(64). In the small-debris regime (Mw,Ew≪1M_{w},E_{w}\ll 1), these two equations in two unknowns (A1′,A2′)(A^{\prime}_{1},A^{\prime}_{2}) generically have a unique solution close to (A1,A2)(A_{1},A_{2}).

Radiation constraints. A structural property of K(m,m) compactons is that the trigonometric integrals I2=∫u​sin⁡x​𝑑xI_{2}=\int u\sin x\,dx and I3=∫u​cos⁡x​𝑑xI_{3}=\int u\cos x\,dx vanish identically for every compacton, regardless of amplitude or position (Proposition 5.3 below). Conservation of I2I_{2} and I3I_{3} therefore constrains the debris alone: I2​[w]=0I_{2}[w]=0 and I3​[w]=0I_{3}[w]=0, forcing the fundamental Fourier mode (k=1k=1) of the debris to vanish.

Nonlocal constraint. The nonlocal momentum I4I_{4} couples the compacton configuration to the debris through the pseudoinverse (Dx2+1)−1(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1}.

Part (c): In an integrable system possessing infinitely many conservation laws of successively higher order, each law constraining a progressively higher moment or Fourier component of the solution (a heuristic correspondence, not a proved structural statement for general integrable systems). The infinite collection leaves no free radiation modes, which is the mechanism underlying the zero-debris theorem [1] (Proposition 5.6). In K(m,m), the hierarchy terminates at five. The debris Fourier modes at wavenumbers k≠1k\neq 1 are unconstrained by any conservation law. The nonlinear collision dynamics naturally excites these modes, and nothing in the conservation structure forces the excitation to vanish. This is the constraint deficit: a finite number of radiation constraints acting on an infinite-dimensional radiation field. ∎

Remark 5.2 (Conditional status and paths to proof).

Theorem 5.1 rests on hypotheses (H1)–(H3), which have different levels of support. Hypothesis (H3) rests on Vodová’s structural classification [46], which rigorously establishes that exactly four local conservation laws exist. The assumption that no additional nonlocal conserved quantities exist beyond I4I_{4} has strong support from the absence of a recursion operator but lacks a formal proof. Hypothesis (H2) follows from Proposition B.2: the cosine-power compacton is the unique positive, symmetric, single-hump compact traveling wave, so any emergent traveling wave with these properties must take this form. Hypothesis (H1) has overwhelming numerical support (three decades of simulations with no counterexamples) but no analytical proof. The main open question is whether collision dynamics necessarily produce traveling-wave structures; orbital stability of K(m,m) compactons (Problem 3 in Appendix K) would resolve this. Despite the conditional status, the theorem provides the first coherent explanation of why K(m,m) collisions produce small but nonzero debris.

Proposition 5.3 (Trigonometric orthogonality).

For every K(m,m) compacton U⁡(ξ)=A​cosα⁡(ξ/ℓ)U(\xi)=A\cos^{\alpha}\!(\xi/\ell) with α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1) and ℓ=2​m/(m−1)\ell=2m/(m-1), the trigonometric conservation integrals vanish:

∫−∞∞U⁡(x−x0)​sin⁡(x)​𝑑x= 0,∫−∞∞U⁡(x−x0)​cos⁡(x)​𝑑x= 0\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}U(x-x_{0})\sin(x)\,dx\;=\;0,\qquad\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}U(x-x_{0})\cos(x)\,dx\;=\;0

for all x0∈ℝx_{0}\in\mathbb{R} and all A>0A>0.

Proof.

Substituting θ=(x−x0)/ℓ\theta=(x-x_{0})/\ell and expanding the trigonometric factor gives ∫U​sin⁡(x)​𝑑x=A​ℓ​sin⁡(x0)​Bα+A​ℓ​cos⁡(x0)​Sα\int U\sin(x)\,dx=A\ell\sin(x_{0})\,B_{\alpha}+A\ell\cos(x_{0})\,S_{\alpha}, where Bα=∫−π/2π/2cosα(θ)cos(ℓθ)dθB_{\alpha}=\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2}\cos^{\alpha}(\theta)\cos(\ell\theta)\,d\theta and SαS_{\alpha} is the corresponding sine integral, which vanishes by parity. The coefficient BαB_{\alpha} is evaluated using the standard Fourier cosine formula

∫0π/2cosa⁡(t)​cos⁡(n​t)​𝑑t=π​Γ​(a+1)2a+1​Γ​(a+n+22)​Γ​(a−n+22).\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{a}(t)\cos(nt)\,dt\;=\;\frac{\pi\,\Gamma(a+1)}{2^{a+1}\,\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{a+n+2}{2}\bigr)\,\Gamma\!\bigl(\tfrac{a-n+2}{2}\bigr)}.

For K(m,m) compactons, ℓ=α+2\ell=\alpha+2, so the second Gamma argument becomes Γ⁡(α−α−2+22)=Γ⁡(0)\Gamma\bigl(\frac{\alpha-\alpha-2+2}{2}\bigr)=\Gamma(0), which has a pole. Since 1/Γ⁡(0)=01/\Gamma(0)=0, the integral Bα=0B_{\alpha}=0 for every α>0\alpha>0. The identity ℓ−α=2\ell-\alpha=2 is a direct consequence of the K(m,m) parameter relations and holds for all m>1m>1. The identical argument applies to ∫U​cos⁡(x)​𝑑x\int U\cos(x)\,dx. Full details appear in Appendix A. ∎

Remark 5.4 (Structural interpretation of Proposition 5.3).

A resonance between the compacton geometry and the trigonometric test functions underlies the vanishing Bα=0B_{\alpha}=0. The compacton support width π​ℓ\pi\ell and the Fourier projection at wavenumber k=1k=1 are related through the identity ℓ=α+2\ell=\alpha+2, which ensures exact cancellation of the position-dependent contributions. This orthogonality transforms the role of I2I_{2} and I3I_{3} in the collision problem: rather than constraining phase shifts, they constrain the debris field directly, requiring its k=1k=1 Fourier component to vanish. The constraint deficit therefore operates entirely on the radiation spectrum, where finitely many constraints (two, from I2I_{2} and I3I_{3}) act on infinitely many debris modes.

Constraint partition.

Table 3 summarizes how the five conservation laws partition between compacton parameters and debris degrees of freedom. The two amplitude-determining constraints (I0I_{0}, I1I_{1}) act on a two-dimensional space, generically forcing amplitude preservation. The two radiation constraints (I2I_{2}, I3I_{3}) act on a single Fourier mode of the debris. The nonlocal law I4I_{4} provides a coupling constraint. In total, five scalar conditions govern an infinite-dimensional post-collision state.

Part (c) is the crux of the constraint deficit argument. In integrable systems, the infinite conservation hierarchy constrains every Fourier mode of the solution: the nn-th conservation law, which involves spatial derivatives of order nn, restricts the nn-th spectral component. The IST translates this algebraic control into perfect elasticity [1]. K(m,m) has no such mechanism. The debris field acquires energy through nonlinear mode coupling during the collision, and only two of its infinitely many spectral components are constrained to vanish afterward.

Numerical confirmation.

Two concrete predictions emerge from the constraint analysis, and both are confirmed by high-resolution spectral analysis of the post-collision debris field (Figure 4). First, the debris Fourier spectrum exhibits a notch at k=1k=1: the fundamental mode is forced to vanish by conservation of I2I_{2} and I3I_{3}, and the measured |w^​(1)||\hat{w}(1)| is suppressed by nearly two orders of magnitude below the spectral peak for all tested values of mm. Second, the debris energy resides predominantly in modes k≥2k\geq 2, with the spectral peak shifting to higher wavenumbers as mm increases (from kpeak≈0.38k_{\mathrm{peak}}\approx 0.38 for m=2m=2 to kpeak≈3.6k_{\mathrm{peak}}\approx 3.6 for m=5m=5), consistent with the narrowing compacton support exciting shorter-wavelength modes during the collision. Grid convergence tests from Nx=256N_{x}=256 through Nx=1024N_{x}=1024 confirm that the notch deepens with refinement while the debris spectrum stabilizes, establishing the notch as a physical feature rather than a numerical artifact. Table 4 summarizes the quantitative results.

The multi-parameter validation of Figure 4 confirms that the k=1k=1 notch is a universal feature of K(mm,mm) collisions: it persists across all tested values of mm, deepening with grid refinement. For m≥3m\geq 3 the debris energy fraction grows with mm (the m=2m=2 case, with its C1C^{1} boundary, sits well over an order of magnitude above), while the notch depth remains consistently deep, and the spectral peak shifts to higher wavenumbers as compacton support narrows.

What the conservation laws do constrain

While the five laws cannot enforce perfect elasticity, they impose strong constraints on what the debris field looks like.

Theorem 5.5 (Conservation Law Constraints on Debris).

For a two-compacton collision in K(m,m) with pre-collision amplitudes A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} and post-collision amplitudes A1′,A2′A^{\prime}_{1},A^{\prime}_{2}, and with the post-collision compactons and the debris field ww of disjoint support (so that the nonlinear energy is additive), the debris field ww satisfies:

  1. (a)

    Debris energy. Ew=Dm​[(A1m+1+A2m+1)−(A1′m+1+A2′m+1)]E_{w}=D_{m}[(A_{1}^{m+1}+A_{2}^{m+1})-(A^{\prime\,m+1}_{1}+A^{\prime\,m+1}_{2})], where DmD_{m} is the energy integral coefficient.

  2. (b)

    Debris mass. Mw=Cm​[(A1+A2)−(A1′+A2′)]M_{w}=C_{m}[(A_{1}+A_{2})-(A^{\prime}_{1}+A^{\prime}_{2})], where CmC_{m} is the mass integral coefficient.

  3. (c)

    Fourier mode constraint. The Fourier transform of the debris at wavenumber k=1k=1 vanishes: w^​(1)=w^​(−1)=0\hat{w}(1)=\hat{w}(-1)=0. All other wavenumbers are unconstrained by conservation laws.

Proof.

Part (a) follows from energy conservation Etot=E1′+E2′+EwE_{\mathrm{tot}}=E^{\prime}_{1}+E^{\prime}_{2}+E_{w} with E⁡[U]=Dm​Am+1E[U]=D_{m}A^{m+1}. Part (b) is analogous using M⁡[U]=Cm​AM[U]=C_{m}A. For (c), conservation of I2I_{2} requires ∫w​sin⁡(x)​𝑑x=I2pre−I2​[comp.​ 1′]−I2​[comp.​ 2′]\int w\sin(x)\,dx=I_{2}^{\mathrm{pre}}-I_{2}[\text{comp.}\ 1^{\prime}]-I_{2}[\text{comp.}\ 2^{\prime}]. By Proposition 5.3, the compacton contributions vanish, and I2pre=0I_{2}^{\mathrm{pre}}=0 as well (since the pre-collision state consists of compactons only). Hence ∫w​sin⁡(x)​𝑑x=0\int w\sin(x)\,dx=0. Since ∫w⁡(x)​sin⁡(x)​𝑑x=−12​i​[w^​(1)−w^​(−1)]\int w(x)\sin(x)\,dx=-\tfrac{1}{2i}[\hat{w}(1)-\hat{w}(-1)] (where w^\hat{w} is the Fourier transform on ℝ\mathbb{R}), and symmetrically ∫w​cos⁡(x)​𝑑x=0\int w\cos(x)\,dx=0 from I3I_{3} conservation gives w^​(1)+w^​(−1)=0\hat{w}(1)+\hat{w}(-1)=0, together these yield w^​(±1)=0\hat{w}(\pm 1)=0. The conservation laws impose no constraint on w^​(k)\hat{w}(k) for k≠±1k\neq\pm 1. ∎

Theorems 5.1 and 5.5 explain the observed collision phenomenology from complementary perspectives. Theorem 5.1 shows why debris exists: the conservation laws constrain only the fundamental Fourier mode of the radiation, leaving all higher modes free. Theorem 5.5 shows what the conservation laws determine: the debris energy, mass, and the vanishing of its dominant spatial frequency. The fifth law (nonlocal momentum) provides an additional coupling constraint. What remains undetermined (the higher Fourier modes and detailed spatial profile of the debris) is governed by the full nonlinear dynamics, not by conservation considerations alone.

Computational methods.

All collision simulations use the spectrally-filtered pseudospectral method described in Appendix D: Nx=512N_{x}=512 grid points, joint LP filtering (Variant C, q=2q=2), biharmonic ramp dissipation with δ=0.15\delta=0.15, and fixed-step RK4 integration. Post-collision amplitudes are extracted by Nelder–Mead least-squares fitting of compacton profiles. Spectral analysis is restricted to wavenumbers below the filter cutoff; see Appendix H for additional detail on debris extraction and signal-to-noise methodology.

5.2 The conservation-elasticity landscape

Contrasting K(m,m) with integrable systems sharpens the collision results of the preceding subsection.

Proposition 5.6 (Integrable Endpoint).

For completely integrable dispersive equations with an infinite hierarchy of independent conservation laws, multi-soliton collisions are perfectly elastic: Ai′=AiA^{\prime}_{i}=A_{i} and Ew=0E_{w}=0.

This classical result [13, 1, 24] follows from the inverse scattering transform: discrete spectral data is preserved under isospectral flow, and pure discrete spectrum excludes radiation.

A second reference point comes from the Benjamin–Bona–Mahony (BBM) equation ut+ux+u​ux−ux​x​t=0u_{t}+u_{x}+uu_{x}-u_{xxt}=0, which possesses exactly three conservation laws [5, 36] and fails every test of integrability. Bona, Pritchard, and Scott [6] demonstrated numerically that BBM solitary wave collisions produce permanent amplitude changes and a trailing dispersive wavetrain. Martel, Merle, and Mizumachi [30] subsequently proved this inelasticity rigorously: for nearly equal BBM solitary waves, the collision generates a dispersive tail whose H1H^{1} norm is bounded below by a positive quantity depending on the amplitude ratio. The Martel–Merle–Mizumachi result establishes that BBM collisions are not perfectly elastic, but it does not specify how the elasticity compares quantitatively with other non-integrable systems.

Why compare BBM and K(m,m)?

The comparison of structurally dissimilar equations is essential for testing whether conservation law count governs collision elasticity as a general principle, or only within particular equation classes. BBM solitary waves have smooth, exponentially decaying tails (sech2\operatorname{sech}^{2} profiles), while K(m,m) compactons have sharp boundaries with the solution vanishing identically beyond finite support. If the conservation-elasticity relationship were controlled by NN alone, the collision character should depend primarily on the number of conservation laws regardless of interaction geometry. If, on the other hand, tail behavior or support structure modulates the relationship, comparing equations with different interaction geometries would reveal this additional dependence. We therefore computed BBM collision elasticity using the same amplitude-based measure (31) applied to K(m,m) in §5.1.

BBM collision simulations.

We solve the BBM equation using a pseudospectral method (Nx=4096N_{x}=4096 grid points, adaptive Runge–Kutta (RK45) time stepping) and measure collision elasticity via (31) across a range of amplitudes and amplitude ratios. Full simulation parameters, validation details, and individual collision measurements appear in Appendix I.

Result.

Across all tested parameter combinations, the BBM collision elasticity satisfies

ℰBBM≈0.9993​–​1.0001,\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{BBM}}\approx 0.9993\text{--}1.0001, (32)

with debris energy fractions of order 10−410^{-4} to 10−510^{-5}. This is comparable to the K(m,m) compacton collisions measured in §5.1, where ℰK⁡(m,m)≈0.999\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{K}(m,m)}\approx 0.999–1.0001.000 despite K(m,m) possessing five conservation laws to BBM’s three. By debris energy the K(m,m) collisions are the cleaner: at A1=1A_{1}=1, A2=0.5A_{2}=0.5 the BBM debris fraction is 1.4×10−41.4\times 10^{-4} (Supplement, Table S3), larger than every K(m,m) value in Table 4.

The result is consistent with the rigorous analysis of Martel, Merle, and Mizumachi, who proved the existence of a nonzero dispersive residual without estimating its magnitude. The near-elasticity of BBM collisions reflects the perturbative nature of interactions between smooth, exponentially localized waves: the overlap region evolves slowly, transferring very little energy to radiation. K(m,m) compactons interact through abrupt contact at their support boundaries, yet they shed less debris energy, consistent with their larger conservation law count.

This single comparison does not separate the effects of conservation law count and interaction geometry: by the amplitude measure the two equations are indistinguishable at the resolution of these runs, and by debris energy the K(m,m) collisions are the cleaner. Other structural differences, such as BBM’s uni-directional phase space, which limits scattering channels, may also contribute. The landscape relating conservation structure to collision outcomes likely depends on several factors.

Taken together, Theorem 5.1, Theorem 5.5, Proposition 5.6, and the BBM comparison place compacton collisions within a broader landscape relating conservation structure and interaction geometry to collision outcomes.

The conservation-elasticity landscape may be richer than a simple monotone relationship between conservation count and elasticity. BBM solitary waves have smooth exponential tails that mediate gradual, perturbative interactions, while K(m,m) compactons interact through abrupt contact at their support boundaries, so the two families differ in interaction geometry as well as in conservation law count. The BBM equation at N=3N=3 collides about as elastically as K(m,m) at N=5N=5 by the amplitude measure, while shedding more debris energy, which leaves open whether geometry modulates the role of the count. This motivates a refined conjecture.

Conjecture 5.7 (Within-Class Conservation-Elasticity Correlation).

For nonlinear dispersive equations sharing a common interaction geometry (solitary wave tail behavior), the collision elasticity ℰ\mathcal{E} at fixed collision parameters is expected to correlate strongly with the number NN of independent conservation laws, with ℰ→1\mathcal{E}\to 1 as N→∞N\to\infty. Across geometric classes, the interaction geometry introduces an independent modulation: equations with smoother, more gradually decaying solitary wave profiles are expected to produce more elastic collisions at equal conservation law count.

The within-class component of Conjecture 5.7 is anchored by two proved endpoints: N=∞N=\infty gives ℰ=1\mathcal{E}=1 (Proposition 5.6), and the constraint deficit of Theorem 5.1 explains why finite NN permits ℰ<1\mathcal{E}<1. Within the K(m,m) family (where all members share the same compact-support geometry), the five conservation laws produce quasi-elastic collisions with ℰ\mathcal{E} within 2×10−32\times 10^{-3} of 11 and debris energy fractions below 4×10−54\times 10^{-5}, close to but not at the integrable endpoint.

The cross-class component remains open. The BBM comparison is not made at equal conservation law count, and it does not isolate geometry: BBM, with three laws, collides about as elastically as K(m,m) by the amplitude measure and sheds more debris energy. A test of the cross-class component needs equation families that share a conservation law count but differ in tail behavior.

Limitations of the evidence.

The within-class monotonicity component rests on one equation family (K(m,m)) and the integrable endpoints; testing with additional families would strengthen the claim. The cross-class component has so far been probed by a single pair (BBM versus K(m,m)), which does not resolve it. Within K(m,m) itself, the case m=3m=3 produces somewhat more elastic collisions than m=2m=2 despite the same conservation law count, suggesting that the specific algebraic forms of the laws influence elasticity beyond the raw count. An additional subtlety, noted by Garralón-López et al. [14], is an odd-even asymmetry in collision robustness across the family. Whether interaction geometry acts as a second independent factor, and if so how it depends on geometric parameters, awaits further investigation (Problem 4 in Appendix K; extended discussion in Appendix I).

5.3 Broader implications: constraint deficit as a general framework

The constraint-deficit mechanism, developed above for K(m,m) compactons, rests on three ingredients that are not specific to any single equation: a finite set of conservation laws, solitary wave solutions parameterized by amplitude and speed, and collisions that produce localized emergent structures plus a radiation field. We conjecture that any dispersive PDE possessing these ingredients admits a constraint-deficit analysis, and that the framework may provide a quantitative lens on the intermediate territory between integrable order and generic nonlinear dynamics.

To make this precise, consider a dispersive PDE with NN independent conservation laws and a family of solitary waves parameterized by a single continuous variable (typically amplitude). After a binary collision, the post-collision state involves two emergent solitary waves (parameterized by 22 amplitudes and 22 phase shifts) and a radiation field with infinitely many degrees of freedom. The NN conservation laws impose Nc=NN_{c}=N scalar constraints on the post-collision state. If Nc≥4N_{c}\geq 4 (two amplitude constraints plus at least two radiation constraints), the emergent amplitudes are generically determined and at least some radiation modes are suppressed. The remaining radiation modes, ∞−(Nc−2)\infty-(N_{c}-2) in a formal count, are unconstrained. As Nc→∞N_{c}\to\infty, all radiation modes become constrained, recovering perfect elasticity: the integrable limit.

This counting argument, which underlies Theorem 5.1, suggests an analogous analysis for any system satisfying the three candidate prerequisites identified from the K(m,m) analysis. One can then define a quantitative measure, the conservation elasticity, capturing the degree to which a finite conservation hierarchy approximates the integrable ideal:

Definition 5.8 (Conservation Elasticity).

For a dispersive PDE with NN independent conservation laws and solitary wave collisions producing debris with energy EwE_{w}, the conservation elasticity is

η⁡(N)= 1−EwEtot,\eta(N)\;=\;1-\frac{E_{w}}{E_{\mathrm{tot}}},

where EtotE_{\mathrm{tot}} is the total energy. The integrable limit corresponds to η=1\eta=1; generic Hamiltonian systems with N=2N=2 yield η≪1\eta\ll 1.

For K(m,m) compactons, η\eta coincides with the energy-based elasticity ℰE\mathcal{E}_{E} of Appendix H. Theorem 4.1 ensures that η\eta and the amplitude-based elasticity ℰ\mathcal{E} are monotonically related, so the within-family ordering is independent of the choice of measure.

The K(m,m) family provides the first systematic test: η\eta ranges from 0.999960.99996 (at m=2m=2) to 0.99999950.9999995 (at m=3m=3) with N=5N=5 (Table 4), while the BBM comparison gives η≈0.9994\eta\approx 0.9994–0.999990.99999 at N=3N=3. Extending this analysis to other families with known conservation counts would begin to map the η\eta-vs-NN relationship.

The broader program of testing the constraint-deficit framework across equation families remains conjectural; we return to this question and its implications in the Concluding Remarks (§8).

6 Compacton emergence from localized initial data

The collision experiments of the preceding section demonstrate that pre-formed compactons survive interaction almost elastically. A complementary question probes the robustness of compactons from the opposite direction: given a localized initial pulse that is not a compacton, does the K(m,m)(m,m) evolution decompose it into compactons? For the integrable KdV equation, the inverse scattering transform provides an exact answer: an arbitrary sufficiently smooth localized initial pulse decomposes into a finite number of solitons whose amplitudes are determined by the Schrödinger eigenvalues of the associated spectral problem [24, 32]. No analogous theory exists for the non-integrable K(m,n)(m,n) family. Numerical experiments reveal, however, that compacton emergence follows strikingly regular patterns.

6.1 Wide-compacton initial data

To avoid Gibbs oscillations associated with discontinuous initial data, we initialize the computation with a wide compacton, the K(m,m)(m,m) compacton shape stretched by a width factor ww:

u0​(x)={A​cosα⁡(x−x0w​ℓ),|x−x0|≤w​π​ℓ/2,0,otherwise,u_{0}(x)=\begin{cases}A\cos^{\alpha}\!\Bigl(\dfrac{x-x_{0}}{w\ell}\Bigr),&|x-x_{0}|\leq w\pi\ell/2,\\[6.0pt] 0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

with α\alpha and ℓ\ell from Theorem 4.1, so that the half-width is ww times the natural half-width π​ℓ/2=m​π/(m−1)\pi\ell/2=m\pi/(m-1). We take w=2.5w=2.5 and A=1A=1 in all cases. This continuous, compactly supported pulse contains sufficient excess width to decompose into multiple compactons while remaining within the class of functions for which the numerical method performs reliably.

6.2 Emergence dynamics

Figure 5 presents the evolution of a wide initial pulse under the K(m,m)(m,m) equation for m=2,3,4,5m=2,3,4,5. In every case, the initial pulse rapidly steepens at the leading edge, sheds compactons from the front, and leaves a dispersive remnant at the rear. By t≈50t\approx 50, three or more distinct compactons have separated, propagating rightward at speeds governed by the universal formula c=m+12​m​Am−1c=\tfrac{m+1}{2m}\,A^{m-1} from Theorem 4.1. The tallest (fastest) compacton leads; progressively smaller compactons trail behind. For m=2m=2, four compactons separate cleanly; for K(3,3)(3,3) a marginal fourth appears at the noise floor (a peak amplitude of 0.080.08, below which peaks are not counted); for m≥4m\geq 4, three are unambiguous while the trailing dynamics fall at or below the numerical noise floor (see below).

Table 5 reports the amplitudes and speeds of the emerged compactons for each K(m,m)(m,m) equation and for the mixed-exponent cases K(2,3)(2,3) and K(3,2)(3,2). Three patterns are evident.

First, the leading compacton speeds are remarkably similar across the K(m,m)(m,m) family, clustering between 0.950.95 and 0.990.99 despite different values of mm. This is an empirical property of the emerged leading amplitudes A1​(m)=1.28,1.20,1.16,1.13A_{1}(m)=1.28,1.20,1.16,1.13, which offset the falling coefficient (m+1)/(2​m)(m+1)/(2m) through the factor A1m−1A_{1}^{m-1}.

Second, trailing compactons separate at rates that depend sensitively on mm. For m=2m=2, the linear speed–amplitude relation c∝Ac\propto A produces moderate speed differences between large and small compactons. For m≥3m\geq 3, the power-law relation c∝Am−1c\propto A^{m-1} causes the smallest resolved compacton to be nearly stationary (c3≤0.12c_{3}\leq 0.12), creating a large speed spread between the leading and trailing structures. This mm-dependent separation rate has no counterpart in the integrable case, where the speed is always linear in amplitude.

Third, the emerged amplitudes are constrained by the conservation laws. The four local conserved quantities (Theorem 4.6), together with I4I_{4} where the initial pulse satisfies u^​(±1)=0\hat{u}(\pm 1)=0 (m=2,4m=2,4 here), relate the initial pulse parameters to the emergent compacton amplitudes. While these constraints cannot determine the amplitudes and positions of N>1N>1 compactons together with the dispersive remnant, they do restrict the set of admissible configurations.

Resolution limit from the regularity hierarchy.

For m≥4m\geq 4, the fourth compacton amplitude is not reported because it falls below the numerical noise floor; for K(3,3)(3,3) it is listed with a dagger. Two competing trends drive this resolution limit. The emerged amplitude A4A_{4} decreases with mm: cleanly resolved at A4=0.11A_{4}=0.11 for K(2,2)(2,2), dropping to A4≈0.10A_{4}\approx 0.10 for K(3,3)(3,3) where it lies near the 0.080.08 noise threshold; no fourth peak is detected for K(4,4)(4,4) or K(5,5)(5,5) at the present spectral resolution. Simultaneously, the Gibbs oscillation amplitude at the compact-support boundary increases with mm, scaling with the boundary regularity exponent α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1). The C1C^{1} boundary at m=2m=2 (α=2\alpha=2) produces negligible Gibbs ringing, while the Hölder boundary at m=5m=5 (α=1/2\alpha=1/2) produces substantial overshoots that propagate as a spurious dispersive wake [9]. These trends cross near m=3m=3, beyond which the expected fourth compacton amplitude lies within or below the spectral noise floor.

This resolution limit is controlled by the same regularity hierarchy that governs the convergence rates of the numerical method [9]: the boundary exponent α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1) simultaneously determines how many compactons can be resolved and how rapidly the scheme converges under grid refinement. Whether a fourth compacton forms for m≥4m\geq 4 cannot be decided at the present spectral resolution.

6.3 Advection–dispersion balance in the mixed-exponent cases

The comparison between K(2,3)(2,3) and K(3,2)(3,2) exposes the role of the advection–dispersion balance in the emergence process. When the advective exponent exceeds the dispersive one (m>nm>n, as in K(3,2)(3,2)), energy concentrates into fewer, taller compactons: K(3,2)(3,2) produces the largest leading amplitude (A1=1.33A_{1}=1.33) and a speed spread across resolved compactons (0.930.93, only three structures resolvable) comparable to the largest K(m,m)(m,m) value. The reverse case m<nm<n (K(2,3)(2,3)) distributes energy more uniformly across the emerged compactons, yielding a narrower amplitude range and the slowest separation of any case tested (c1−c4=0.75c_{1}-c_{4}=0.75).

This asymmetry admits a physical interpretation. The exponent mm controls nonlinear steepening at the compacton peak, where u∼O⁡(1)u\sim O(1), while the exponent nn governs dispersive spreading at the edges, where u≪1u\ll 1. Stronger advection relative to dispersion favors the formation of coherent, high-amplitude structures.

6.4 Implications for the structure-beyond-integrability framework

The emergence experiments provide a third line of evidence, alongside the universal formulas (Theorem 4.1) and the quasi-elastic collisions (§5), that the K(m,m)(m,m) equations possess more structure than a generic non-integrable system. In particular:

  1. 1.

    Direct measurement of the leading compacton’s propagation speed (by linear regression of peak positions across snapshots at t=100,125,150,175t=100,125,150,175) confirms the universal formula c=[(m+1)/(2​m)]​Am−1c=[(m+1)/(2m)]\,A^{m-1} to within 1%1\% for all four K(m,m)(m,m) cases. For the mixed-exponent cases the leading speed obeys the exact traveling-wave relation c=[(n+1)/(m+n)]​Am−1c=[(n+1)/(m+n)]\,A^{m-1}, obtained from the crest of the first integral of the K(m,n)(m,n) profile equation; the exact speed equals the K(m,m)(m,m) prediction, evaluated with the advective exponent mm, times the factor 2​m​(n+1)/[(m+n)​(m+1)]2m(n+1)/[(m+n)(m+1)], that is 1.0671.067 (+6.7%+6.7\%) for K(2,3)(2,3) and 0.9000.900 (−10.0%-10.0\%) for K(3,2)(3,2); the directly measured leading speeds then agree with the exact relation to within 0.7%0.7\% for K(2,3)(2,3) and 3.1%3.1\% for K(3,2)(3,2) (Supplement, Table S6).

  2. 2.

    The leading compacton speed c1c_{1} is approximately independent of mm for unit-amplitude initial data, varying only between 0.950.95 and 0.990.99 across m∈{2,3,4,5}m\in\{2,3,4,5\}, a universality not predicted by any existing theory.

  3. 3.

    The emergence process respects the four local conservation laws of Theorem 4.6 (and I4I_{4} for m=2,4m=2,4, where the initial pulse lies in its domain), and the constraint-deficit mechanism of Theorem 5.5 should apply to the dispersive remnant left behind.

Developing a predictive theory for compacton emergence (analogous to inverse scattering for KdV) remains an open problem. The numerical results in Table 5 provide quantitative targets for such a theory. A natural first step would be to establish whether the number of emerged compactons depends on any calculable property of the initial pulse (its mass I0I_{0}, energy I1I_{1}, or some analogue of the Schrödinger eigenvalue count).

7 Traveling waves on a positive background

The compactons studied in Sections 4 and 3 arise as traveling waves on a zero background: the undisturbed state is u=0u=0, and the wave amplitude returns to zero at finite distance. A natural generalization replaces the zero background with a constant positive shelf u=a>0u=a>0 and seeks traveling wave solutions of the form

u⁡(x,t)=a+f⁡(x−c​t),a>0,f⁡(ξ)→0​as​|ξ|→∞.u(x,t)=a+f(x-ct),\qquad a>0,\quad f(\xi)\to 0\ \text{as}\ |\xi|\to\infty. (33)

This extension has physical motivation: real wave phenomena rarely occur on quiescent backgrounds, and the positive shelf introduces a characteristic scale that interacts nontrivially with the nonlinear dispersion. It also has mathematical motivation: the background parameter aa controls a bifurcation in the traveling wave phase portrait that reveals the compacton as a singular limit of smooth solitary and periodic waves.

The analysis reinforces the constraint-deficit framework of §5.1. The compacton’s emergence as an isolated object (not part of a continuous family of smooth traveling waves) explains why collision outcomes cannot smoothly interpolate between elastic and inelastic: the compacton is structurally rigid, and any perturbation either preserves it or generates debris. The singular limit analysis provides independent confirmation of the compacton’s special status within the K(m,m) traveling-wave landscape.

Lax’s theory of KdV periodic solutions [25] constructs NN-phase quasi-periodic waves, which reduce to cnoidal waves for N=1N=1, by variational methods, using the infinitely many conserved functionals FjF_{j} in involution [26]. The solutions lie on NN-dimensional invariant tori, parametrized by spectral data from the associated Schrödinger operator. A central question for the non-integrable K(m,m) family is: what periodic wave structure survives when the infinite conservation hierarchy collapses to a finite set?

This section answers that question through a systematic phase-plane analysis. The main results are: a critical speed formula c∗=m​am−1c^{*}=ma^{m-1} that separates solitary from periodic behavior (§7.2); explicit first-integral and quadrature formulas for K(2,2) shelf waves (§7.3); a singular limit theorem showing how the compacton emerges through simultaneous loss of regularity and support compactification (§7.4); and a precise comparison between the resulting one-parameter periodic families and the rich multi-dimensional torus structure of Lax’s integrable theory (§7.5).

7.1 Hamiltonian reduction and the vv-variable

Substituting the traveling waves f⁡(x−c​t)f(x-ct) on a shelf a>0a>0, u=a+fu=a+f, into the K(m,m) equation (8), writing ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct, and integrating once yields

−c⁡(a+f)+(a+f)m+[(a+f)m]′′=C0,-c(a+f)+(a+f)^{m}+\bigl[(a+f)^{m}\bigr]^{\prime\prime}=C_{0}, (34)

where the integration constant C0=−c​a+amC_{0}=-ca+a^{m} is determined by the boundary condition f→0f\to 0, f′→0f^{\prime}\to 0 as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty. Rearranging gives a second-order ODE for the total field a+fa+f.

The equation simplifies through the substitution

v=(a+f)m,v=(a+f)^{m}, (35)

which converts the degenerate-dispersion structure into polynomial form. Since a+f>0a+f>0 for shelf waves (the field remains above zero), this change of variable is a smooth diffeomorphism. In the vv-variable, equation (34) becomes

v′′+V′​(v)=0,v^{\prime\prime}+V^{\prime}(v)=0, (36)

where the potential is

V⁡(v)=12​v2−c​mm+1​v(m+1)/m+(c​a−am)​v.\boxed{V(v)=\frac{1}{2}\,v^{2}-\frac{cm}{m+1}\,v^{(m+1)/m}+(ca-a^{m})\,v.} (37)

Equation (36) is a Hamiltonian ODE with conserved energy

E=12​(v′)2+V⁡(v).E=\tfrac{1}{2}(v^{\prime})^{2}+V(v). (38)

When a=0a=0, the substitution v=umv=u^{m} is singular at u=0u=0: this is the point where the degenerate dispersion coefficient um−1u^{m-1} vanishes and compact support becomes possible. For a>0a>0, the total field remains strictly positive and the vv-variable provides a globally smooth coordinate. The transition a→0+a\to 0^{+} transforms the smooth Hamiltonian system into a degenerate one, a mechanism we analyze in §7.4.

7.2 Phase-plane classification

The equilibria of (36) satisfy V′​(v)=0V^{\prime}(v)=0. Direct computation gives V′​(v)=v−c​v1/m+(c​a−am)V^{\prime}(v)=v-c\,v^{1/m}+(ca-a^{m}), and substitution of v0=amv_{0}=a^{m} confirms that V′​(am)=0V^{\prime}(a^{m})=0 for every cc and a>0a>0. This is the equilibrium corresponding to the undisturbed shelf f=0f=0.

Theorem 7.1 (Critical speed and equilibrium classification).

For K(m,m) with m≥2m\geq 2 and shelf height a>0a>0, define the critical speed

c∗=m​am−1.\boxed{c^{*}=m\,a^{m-1}.} (39)

The equilibrium v0=amv_{0}=a^{m} of the potential (37) has the following character:

  1. (a)

    If c<c∗c<c^{*}, then V′′​(v0)>0V^{\prime\prime}(v_{0})>0 and v0v_{0} is a center: the phase plane contains a family of nested periodic orbits.

  2. (b)

    If c=c∗c=c^{*}, then V′′​(v0)=0V^{\prime\prime}(v_{0})=0 and v0v_{0} is a degenerate equilibrium.

  3. (c)

    If c>c∗c>c^{*}, then V′′​(v0)<0V^{\prime\prime}(v_{0})<0 and v0v_{0} is a saddle point: the phase plane contains a homoclinic orbit enclosing the region v0<v<v1v_{0}<v<v_{1}.

Proof.

Differentiating V′​(v)=v−c​v1/m+(c​a−am)V^{\prime}(v)=v-c\,v^{1/m}+(ca-a^{m}) yields

V′′​(v)=1−cm​v(1−m)/m.V^{\prime\prime}(v)=1-\frac{c}{m}\,v^{(1-m)/m}. (40)

At v0=amv_{0}=a^{m}, this evaluates to V′′​(am)=1−c/(m​am−1)=1−c/c∗V^{\prime\prime}(a^{m})=1-c/(m\,a^{m-1})=1-c/c^{*}. The sign of V′′​(am)V^{\prime\prime}(a^{m}) determines the character of the equilibrium: positive gives a center (restoring force), negative gives a saddle (repelling), and zero gives the degenerate boundary case. ∎

The critical speed formula encodes a competition between the propagation velocity cc and the effective dispersion speed m​am−1ma^{m-1} set by the shelf height. When the wave travels faster than this threshold, the shelf equilibrium becomes unstable and a localized excursion (solitary wave) is possible. When it travels more slowly, the equilibrium is stable and only oscillatory (periodic) solutions exist near it.

Theorem 7.2 (Existence of solitary and periodic waves).

Under the hypotheses of Theorem 7.1:

  1. (a)

    Solitary waves. For c>c∗c>c^{*}, the energy surface E=V⁡(am)E=V(a^{m}) contains a unique homoclinic orbit in the half-plane v>0v>0. In the original variable, u=a+fu=a+f where f⁡(ξ)>0f(\xi)>0 with f⁡(ξ)→0f(\xi)\to 0 exponentially as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty. The profile is C∞C^{\infty} and symmetric about its maximum.

  2. (b)

    Periodic waves. For c<c∗c<c^{*}, a one-parameter family of periodic orbits exists near v0=amv_{0}=a^{m}, parametrized by energy E∈(V⁡(v0),Emax)E\in(V(v_{0}),E_{\mathrm{max}}). The period satisfies T⁡(E)→2​π/ω0T(E)\to 2\pi/\omega_{0} as E→V​(v0)+E\to V(v_{0})^{+} and T⁡(E)→∞T(E)\to\infty as E→EmaxE\to E_{\mathrm{max}} if am−1<c<c∗a^{m-1}<c<c^{*}, where Emax=V⁡(vs)E_{\mathrm{max}}=V(v_{s}) at the saddle vs>0v_{s}>0; if 0<c≤am−10<c\leq a^{m-1} there is no saddle in v>0v>0, the family ends at the orbit through v=0v=0 with Emax=V⁡(0)E_{\mathrm{max}}=V(0), and T⁡(Emax)T(E_{\mathrm{max}}) is finite (equal to 2​π​m/(m−1)2\pi m/(m-1) at c=am−1c=a^{m-1}). Here

    ω0=V′′​(am)=1−c/(m​am−1).\omega_{0}=\sqrt{V^{\prime\prime}(a^{m})}=\sqrt{1-c/(m\,a^{m-1})}. (41)
Proof.

Part (a): When c>c∗c>c^{*}, the equilibrium v0=amv_{0}=a^{m} is a saddle. The separatrix energy is Esep=V⁡(am)E_{\mathrm{sep}}=V(a^{m}). On the level set E=EsepE=E_{\mathrm{sep}}, the equation V⁡(v)=V⁡(am)V(v)=V(a^{m}) with v>amv>a^{m} has a unique positive root v1v_{1} (the crest value), because V⁡(v)→+∞V(v)\to+\infty as v→+∞v\to+\infty while V⁡(v)<V⁡(am)V(v)<V(a^{m}) for vv slightly above ama^{m}. The resulting homoclinic orbit connects the saddle to itself through the excursion v0→v1→v0v_{0}\to v_{1}\to v_{0}. Symmetry of the orbit follows from the time-reversibility ξ↦−ξ\xi\mapsto-\xi of (36). Smoothness is inherited from the smooth Hamiltonian flow away from the singular set v=0v=0, which the orbit never approaches since v≥am>0v\geq a^{m}>0.

Part (b): Standard Hamiltonian center theory. The Lyapunov center theorem guarantees a family of periodic orbits near any non-degenerate center. The period formula follows from the quadrature T⁡(E)=2​∫vminvmax𝑑v/2​(E−V​(v))T(E)=2\int_{v_{\min}}^{v_{\max}}dv/\sqrt{2(E-V(v))}, and the stated limits are standard consequences of the linearization frequency ω0\omega_{0} and the logarithmic divergence of the integral near the separatrix when a saddle bounds the family; for c≤am−1c\leq a^{m-1} the boundary orbit reaches v=0v=0, where the integrand behaves like v−1/2v^{-1/2} for c<am−1c<a^{m-1} and like v−(m+1)/(2m)v^{-(m+1)/(2m)} at c=am−1c=a^{m-1}, integrable in both cases, so the limiting period is finite. ∎

The next result strengthens part (b) of Theorem 7.2 by establishing strict monotonicity of the period function.

Proposition 7.3 (Period monotonicity).

For m=2,3m=2,3 and every c∈(0,c∗)c\in(0,c^{*}), the period function T⁡(E)T(E) of the K(m,m) periodic family is strictly increasing: T′​(E)>0T^{\prime}(E)>0 for all E∈(V⁡(v0),Emax)E\in(V(v_{0}),E_{\mathrm{max}}).

V′​(v0)=0,V′′​(v0)=1−cc∗>0,c∗=m​am−1.V^{\prime}(v_{0})=0,\qquad V^{\prime\prime}(v_{0})=1-\frac{c}{c^{*}}>0,\qquad c^{*}=m\,a^{m-1}.
