These two families, separated by the critical speed c=c∗c=c^{*} at which the solitary-wave branch terminates (Remark 7.5), organize into the classification shown in Table 6, Figure 6, and the phase portraits of Figure 7 and Supplement, Figure S1. The bifurcation between these regimes in the (a,c)(a,c) parameter plane is shown in the bifurcation diagram (Supplement, Figure S3).

Remark 7.4 (Structural instability of compactons).

Any positive perturbation of the background, however small, transforms the compacton into a C∞C^{\infty} solitary wave with exponential tails. The compact-support wave exists only at the singular endpoint a=0a=0 of the parameter family. This contrasts with KdV solitons, which are smoothly embedded in the cnoidal wave family: the sech2 profile deforms continuously into Jacobi elliptic cnoidal waves as the modulus varies. For K(m,m), the analogous deformation involves a discontinuous change in both regularity and support structure.

Remark 7.5 (The critical speed c=c∗c=c^{*}).

At c=c∗=m​am−1c=c^{*}=m\,a^{m-1} the center and saddle equilibria of VV coalesce in a saddle-node bifurcation: V′​(am)=V′′​(am)=0V^{\prime}(a^{m})=V^{\prime\prime}(a^{m})=0 while V′′′​(am)=(m−1)/(m​am)>0V^{\prime\prime\prime}(a^{m})=(m-1)/(m\,a^{m})>0, so v0=amv_{0}=a^{m} is a stationary inflection point of VV. The homoclinic orbit does not survive. As c→c∗+c\to{c^{*}}^{+} the solitary wave broadens (κ→0\kappa\to 0) and flattens, its amplitude vanishing linearly,

fmax∼3​a​(c−c∗)(m−1)​c∗,f_{\max}\sim\frac{3a\,(c-c^{*})}{(m-1)\,c^{*}},

which for K(2,2) is the onset behavior of (50). At c=c∗c=c^{*} itself VV is strictly increasing for v>0v>0, so an orbit with a+f>0a+f>0 that leaves the shelf cannot return to it. The level set E=V⁡(am)E=V(a^{m}) carries only a one-sided front of depression, which approaches the shelf algebraically, f(ξ)∼−12a/((m−1)ξ2)f(\xi)\sim-12a/\bigl((m-1)\,\xi^{2}\bigr), with exponent −2-2 for every mm, and reaches u=0u=0 at finite ξ\xi with infinite slope. The critical curve c=c∗​(a)c=c^{*}(a) is therefore the codimension-one boundary between the solitary wave regime (c>c∗c>c^{*}, exponential tails) and the periodic regime (c<c∗c<c^{*}, center oscillations); no solitary wave lies on it.

7.3 Exact reduction for K(2,2)

The simplest member of the family, K(2,2): ut+(u2)x+(u2)x​x​x=0u_{t}+(u^{2})_{x}+(u^{2})_{xxx}=0, admits the most complete analytical reduction within the family, illustrating the general theory while revealing the limits of closed-form analysis. Setting w=a+fw=a+f (the total field) and m=2m=2, the potential (37) becomes

V⁡(v)=12​v2−2​c3​v3/2+(c​a−a2)​v,V(v)=\frac{1}{2}\,v^{2}-\frac{2c}{3}\,v^{3/2}+(ca-a^{2})\,v, (42)

with equilibrium at v0=a2v_{0}=a^{2} and critical speed c∗=2​ac^{*}=2a.

First integral and factored form

An alternative approach works directly with the total-field variable w=vw=\sqrt{v} (equivalently, v=w2v=w^{2}).11 1 The symbol ww is reused here for the total-field variable; it should not be confused with the debris field w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) of §5.1. The K(2,2) traveling wave ODE in the ww-variable reads

−c​w+w2+2​w​w′′+2​(w′)2+(c​a−a2)=0.-cw+w^{2}+2w\,w^{\prime\prime}+2(w^{\prime})^{2}+(ca-a^{2})=0. (43)

Treating (w′)2(w^{\prime})^{2} as a dependent variable and solving the resulting linear ODE yields a first integral

(w′)2=c​w3−w24−c​a−a22+Dw2,(w^{\prime})^{2}=\frac{cw}{3}-\frac{w^{2}}{4}-\frac{ca-a^{2}}{2}+\frac{D}{w^{2}}, (44)

where the constant D=c​a3/6−a4/4D=ca^{3}/6-a^{4}/4 is fixed by the boundary conditions w→aw\to a, w′→0w^{\prime}\to 0 as |ξ|→∞|\xi|\to\infty.

For K(2,2), the compacton limit can be verified explicitly. Setting a=0a=0 in the first integral (44) gives D=0D=0, so (w′)2=c​w/3−w2/4(w^{\prime})^{2}=cw/3-w^{2}/4, with solution

w0​(ξ)=4​c3​cos2⁡(ξ4),|ξ|≤2​π,w_{0}(\xi)=\frac{4c}{3}\cos^{2}\!\left(\frac{\xi}{4}\right),\qquad|\xi|\leq 2\pi, (45)

recovering the standard K(2,2) compacton [15].

For a>0a>0, however, the first integral does not yield an explicit profile w⁡(ξ)w(\xi). Multiplying (44) by 4​w24w^{2} and factoring the resulting quartic polynomial produces the central identity of this section. Since w=aw=a is a double root (reflecting the boundary condition w→aw\to a, w′→0w^{\prime}\to 0), the quartic takes the form

4​w2​(w′)2=(w−a)2​(w+−w)​(w−w−),\boxed{4w^{2}(w^{\prime})^{2}=(w-a)^{2}\,(w_{+}-w)\,(w-w_{-}),} (46)

where w±w_{\pm} are the roots of the residual quadratic

Q⁡(w)=w2+(2​a−4​c3)​w+(a2−2​c​a3).Q(w)=w^{2}+\Bigl(2a-\frac{4c}{3}\Bigr)\,w+\Bigl(a^{2}-\frac{2ca}{3}\Bigr). (47)

The discriminant of QQ simplifies to

ΔQ=8​c9​(2​c−3​a),\Delta_{Q}=\frac{8c}{9}\,(2c-3a), (48)

which is positive for all c>c∗=2​a>0c>c^{*}=2a>0. The two roots are

w±=2​c3−a±13​2​c​(2​c−3​a),w_{\pm}=\frac{2c}{3}-a\pm\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{2c(2c-3a)}\,, (49)

with w+>aw_{+}>a giving the separatrix crest (the maximum value attained on the homoclinic orbit) and w−<0w_{-}<0 lying in the unphysical half-plane. The double root at w=aw=a reflects the saddle-point structure at the shelf equilibrium, and the orbit oscillates between w=aw=a and w=w+w=w_{+}.

Solitary wave properties

From the factored form (46), the solitary wave profile has the following properties.

The peak excursion above the shelf is

fmax=w+−a=2​c3−2​a+13​2​c​(2​c−3​a).\boxed{f_{\max}=w_{+}-a=\frac{2c}{3}-2a+\frac{1}{3}\sqrt{2c(2c-3a)}\,.} (50)

In the vv-variable, the crest value is v1=w+2v_{1}=w_{+}^{2}, which lies above the second equilibrium vc=(c−a)2v_{c}=(c-a)^{2}: the separatrix overshoots the center before returning to the saddle. In the compacton limit a→0a\to 0, the formula reduces to fmax→4​c/3f_{\max}\to 4c/3, recovering the known K(2,2) compacton amplitude.

The exponential decay rate, determined by linearization of the Hamiltonian system about the saddle, is

κ=c−2​a2​a,\kappa=\sqrt{\frac{c-2a}{2a}}, (51)

so that f⁡(ξ)≈A​e−κ​|ξ|f(\xi)\approx A\,e^{-\kappa|\xi|} for large |ξ||\xi|, where AA depends on aa and cc. As a→0+a\to 0^{+}, the decay rate κ→∞\kappa\to\infty: the exponential tails steepen without bound, approaching the vertical cutoff of the compacton.

Non-sech2 profile and quadrature

Testing any sech2 ansatz against (46) reveals an obstruction: the right-hand side factors as (w−a)2​(w+−w)​(w−w−)(w-a)^{2}(w_{+}-w)(w-w_{-}) with distinct linear terms rather than a perfect square. The exact profile is therefore not sech2 and must be obtained by implicit quadrature:

ξ=±∫w⁡(ξ)w+2​w′​d​w′(w′−a)​(w+−w′)​(w′−w−).\xi=\pm\int_{w(\xi)}^{w_{+}}\frac{2w^{\prime}\,dw^{\prime}}{(w^{\prime}-a)\sqrt{(w_{+}-w^{\prime})(w^{\prime}-w_{-})}}\,. (52)

This non-standard character is a direct consequence of the nonlinear dispersion in K(2,2), which produces a v3/2v^{3/2} term in the potential rather than the cubic responsible for KdV’s sech2 profiles. Periodic waves

For c<c∗=2​ac<c^{*}=2a, the equilibrium v0=a2v_{0}=a^{2} is a center, and the phase portrait contains a family of nested periodic orbits with small-amplitude period T0=2​π/1−c/(2​a)T_{0}=2\pi/\sqrt{1-c/(2a)}, which diverges as c→(2​a)−c\to(2a)^{-}. In the ww-variable the first integral is a quartic polynomial P4​(w)P_{4}(w), so the cnoidal profiles are given implicitly by elliptic integrals. They are not the Jacobi cn2\mathrm{cn}^{2} profiles of KdV: the v3/2v^{3/2} term in the potential makes the integrand w​d​w/P4​(w)w\,dw/\sqrt{P_{4}(w)} rather than d​w/P4​(w)dw/\sqrt{P_{4}(w)}. Detailed period-energy analysis appears in Appendix J.

7.4 The singular limit: from shelf waves to compactons

The most revealing feature of the shelf-wave family is the behavior as a→0+a\to 0^{+}. The background vanishes, the smooth Hamiltonian system degenerates, and the compacton appears as a singular endpoint of the one-parameter family of solitary waves. The following theorem makes this precise.

Figure 8 illustrates the progressive steepening of the wave tails as a→0+a\to 0^{+} for K(2,2).

7.5 Periodic waves and the legacy of Lax (1975)

In one of the foundational papers of integrable systems theory, Lax [25] constructed periodic solutions of the KdV equation through a variational principle: minimize the conserved functional FN+1F_{N+1} subject to the constraints Fj=AjF_{j}=A_{j} for j=−1,0,…,N−1j=-1,0,\ldots,N-1. The solutions lie on NN-dimensional invariant tori and are almost periodic in time. The simplest case N=1N=1 recovers the classical cnoidal waves. The 1976 companion [26] reviewed the construction and extended it to minimax critical points, and in its appendix the present author computed the N=2N=2 case numerically, observing that the solution resumed its initial shape, in a shifted position, after a finite time.22 2 I had just arrived at the Courant Institute as a first-year graduate student when Peter Lax asked me to compute the almost periodic cnoidal waves of the KdV equation. The experience had a profound impact on my career and, eventually, led to this paper.

The variational characterization extends formally to K(m,m): traveling waves satisfy δ​ℋ/δ​u=c​δ​P/δ​u+κ\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta u=c\,\delta P/\delta u+\kappa with κ∈ker⁡𝔇\kappa\in\ker\mathfrak{D} (§4.4), which is the N=1N=1 case of Lax’s constrained optimization. The fundamental difference lies in the dimension of the resulting solution families.

Finite conservation and one-parameter families

Lax’s construction of NN-dimensional tori requires N+1N+1 functionally independent conserved functionals in involution. For KdV, the infinite hierarchy {Fj}j=−1∞\{F_{j}\}_{j=-1}^{\infty} provides this for arbitrary NN, and Lax’s Theorem 5.6 of [25] establishes that the resulting solution set is an NN-dimensional manifold.

For K(m,m) with m≥2m\geq 2, the mechanism behind Lax’s construction is absent. The equation carries five known conservation laws (Theorem 4.6), but, lacking a recursion operator, they do not extend to an infinite hierarchy, and although the five are in involution (§4.3), three of them are Casimirs of 𝔇\mathfrak{D}, which generate no flow. The two remaining functionals, ℋ\mathcal{H} and PP, generate the time flow and spatial translation, and their relative equilibria, δ​ℋ/δ​u=c​δ​P/δ​u+κ\delta\mathcal{H}/\delta u=c\,\delta P/\delta u+\kappa, are the traveling waves: precisely Lax’s N=1N=1 case. The construction therefore yields one-parameter families of periodic orbits, parametrized by a single energy value. No two-parameter families arise from it, no invariant tori of dimension greater than one are furnished by this mechanism, and the angle-action variables of the integrable theory have no counterpart.

Table 7 collects the parallel and divergent features.

What survives without integrability

The traveling wave ODE is Hamiltonian for K(m,m) just as for KdV, generating one-parameter periodic families by the standard center theorem with variational characterization as constrained extremals of HH subject to fixed PP. The period function T⁡(E)T(E) increases monotonically from T0T_{0} to TmaxT_{\max}, with Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty only for c>am−1c>a^{m-1} (Proposition 7.3, for m=2,3m=2,3; Supplement, Figure S2).

What does not survive is the multi-dimensional structure: without the infinite hierarchy in involution, there is no infinite family of commuting flows, no angle-action coordinates, no spectral characterization through finite-gap potentials. The KdV periodic theory lives on finite-dimensional invariant tori; the K(m,m) periodic theory lives on one-dimensional energy curves.

The compacton as singular endpoint

In Lax’s theory, the KdV soliton appears as the T→∞T\to\infty limit of cnoidal waves: the elliptic modulus k→1k\to 1, but the solution remains analytic throughout. For K(m,m), the corresponding limit is far more singular: regularity loss (C∞C^{\infty} to the compacton’s boundary class; see Table 1), and support compactification occur simultaneously (Theorem 7.6). This double singularity, which has no analogue in Lax’s integrable theory, arises from the degenerate dispersion coefficient um−1u^{m-1} vanishing at u=0u=0. The compacton is not merely a limiting wave profile but a point where the Hamiltonian structure of the traveling wave ODE undergoes qualitative degeneration.

8 Concluding remarks

Lax’s 1968 discovery that operator compatibility conditions can unlock the complete analytical structure of nonlinear dispersive equations [24, 13, 1] naturally raises the question of what structure persists when that compatibility fails.

The K(m,m) compacton family provides a concrete answer. These equations fail every test of complete integrability (§3): no Lax pair exists, the Painlevé property fails, the symmetry algebra is finite-dimensional, and the conservation hierarchy terminates. Yet substantial mathematical organization persists. Universal algebraic formulas govern all compacton parameters through a single exponent (Theorem 4.1). These formulas yield consequences that had not been previously identified: the trigonometric conservation integrals vanish on every K(m,m) compacton (Proposition 5.3), the cosine-power ansatz is exclusive to the diagonal m=nm=n (Proposition B.1), and the mass and translation generator increase along the compacton family for all m>1m>1 (Corollary 4.5). Five known independent conservation laws (exactly four local and one nonlocal) constrain the dynamics in ways that are both strong enough to produce quasi-elastic collisions and too weak to enforce perfect elasticity. The constraint-deficit analysis (Theorem 5.1) shows that while these laws constrain emergent amplitudes and force the fundamental Fourier mode of collision debris to vanish, all higher radiation modes remain unconstrained. Recent high-resolution numerical studies [14, 16] have independently confirmed and extended this quasi-elastic picture, revealing additional structure, including odd-even asymmetry in collision robustness, that the analytical framework accommodates but does not yet fully explain. The analysis generates testable predictions, including a k=1k=1 notch in the debris spectrum and a spectral peak shift with increasing mm, both of which are confirmed numerically across m=2,3,4,5m=2,3,4,5 (Figure 4). Hamiltonian geometry provides variational principles and stability theory despite the absence of a bi-Hamiltonian pair.

The shelf-wave analysis of §7 adds a further dimension: traveling waves on a positive background u=a>0u=a>0 organize into a phase-plane classification governed by the critical speed c∗=m​am−1c^{*}=m\,a^{m-1}, with smooth solitary waves for c>c∗c>c^{*} and one-parameter cnoidal families for c<c∗c<c^{*}. The compacton emerges as a singular limit a→0+a\to 0^{+} in which two structures collapse simultaneously: regularity drops (C∞C^{\infty} to the compacton’s boundary class), and the support compactifies. This double singularity has no analogue in Lax’s integrable periodic theory. The finite conservation hierarchy limits the periodic waves to one-parameter families on energy curves, a stark reduction from the NN-dimensional tori of the KdV theory [25, 26].

This is not residual integrability; it is a different organizing principle for the K(m,m) family, one in which scaling universality and finite conservation structure replace the spectral machinery of the IST.

Implications for future research.

The constraint-deficit framework yields concrete predictions, two of which have been confirmed numerically. The predicted spectral notch at wavenumber k=1k=1 in collision debris and the systematic peak shift with increasing mm are both verified across all tested values (Figure 4, Table 4). The BBM collision experiments (§5.2) found BBM collisions about as elastic as K(m,m) collisions by the amplitude measure, with more debris energy, leaving open whether interaction geometry modulates the role of conservation count (Conjecture 5.7). Beyond K(m,m), the methods employed here (pattern recognition across parameter families, conservation counting, constraint analysis of collision outcomes, and phase-plane uniqueness arguments) could in principle apply to other systems with finite conservation structure, though each case would require independent verification.

Most physically relevant nonlinear dispersive systems are not completely integrable. Whether the K(m,m) family is representative of a broader class remains an open question; the territory between integrable order and generic chaos may be richer than the integrable/non-integrable dichotomy suggests, but this paper establishes structure only for K(m,m). The BBM collision study reported here provided one such test; extending these comparisons to additional equation families with known conservation counts, and developing the stability theory for singular compacton profiles, are natural next steps that would clarify the scope of these ideas. The eight problems posed in Appendix K outline a research program aimed at understanding mathematical structure beyond the integrable paradigm.

Lax showed what structure looks like when integrability succeeds. The K(m,m) equations show what structure looks like when it fails. Between these poles lies a vast landscape of nonlinear dispersive systems, most of which are not completely integrable, where the question is not whether structure exists but what form it takes. The constraint-deficit framework, the conservation-elasticity landscape, and the singular limit analysis developed here offer partial answers for one family of equations. Extending these ideas to the broader territory remains the central challenge.

Peter Lax approached mathematical problems with a conviction that the right viewpoint would reveal hidden order, and that computation and theory were partners in this search. The work presented here, which combines numerical experiment with analytical proof to uncover organizing principles in a non-integrable system, is offered in the same spirit. The search for structure in nonlinear phenomena, wherever it may be found, continues the tradition that Lax established.

Nonlocal momentum (I4I_{4}) decomposes as I4=I4self​(A1′)+I4self​(A2′)+I4cross​(Δ)+I4debrisI_{4}=I_{4}^{\mathrm{self}}(A^{\prime}_{1})+I_{4}^{\mathrm{self}}(A^{\prime}_{2})+I_{4}^{\mathrm{cross}}(\Delta)+I_{4}^{\mathrm{debris}}, where I4selfI_{4}^{\mathrm{self}} depends on amplitude alone (by translation invariance of the self-interaction kernel), I4crossI_{4}^{\mathrm{cross}} depends on the inter-compacton separation Δ\Delta, and I4debrisI_{4}^{\mathrm{debris}} involves the debris field. For asymptotically separated post-collision compactons, I4cross=0I_{4}^{\mathrm{cross}}=0 (the supports are disjoint and u^​(±1)=0\hat{u}(\pm 1)=0 for each compacton), so I4I_{4} conservation reduces to a constraint coupling I4self​(A1′)+I4self​(A2′)I_{4}^{\mathrm{self}}(A^{\prime}_{1})+I_{4}^{\mathrm{self}}(A^{\prime}_{2}) with I4debrisI_{4}^{\mathrm{debris}}. Since I4self∝A2I_{4}^{\mathrm{self}}\propto A^{2} (the kernel integral is bilinear), amplitude preservation Ai′=AiA^{\prime}_{i}=A_{i} automatically satisfies the compacton part, and the constraint passes to the debris.

In summary, the five conservation laws constrain the emergent amplitudes (given the debris contribution) and suppress a single Fourier mode of the debris. The infinitely many remaining debris degrees of freedom (all Fourier modes with k≠1k\neq 1) are governed by the nonlinear collision dynamics alone. This stands in contrast to integrable systems, where the nn-th conservation law in the infinite hierarchy constrains the nn-th spectral degree of freedom, leaving no unconstrained radiation modes.

Appendix B Structural extensions

B.1 The cosine-power ansatz and K(m,m) exclusivity

Theorem 4.1 establishes universal formulas for K(m,m) compactons via the cosine-power ansatz U⁡(ξ)=A​cosα⁡(ξ/ℓ)U(\xi)=A\cos^{\alpha}(\xi/\ell). A natural question is whether this ansatz extends to the broader K(m,n) family with m≠nm\neq n.

Proposition B.1 (Cosine-power exclusivity).

Within the K(m,n) equation family with m,n>1m,n>1, the cosine-power ansatz (12) produces valid traveling wave solutions if and only if m=nm=n.

Proof.

The K(m,n) traveling wave ODE, after one integration, reads

−c​U+Um+(Un)′′=0.-cU+U^{m}+(U^{n})^{\prime\prime}=0. (58)

Substituting U=A​cosα⁡θU=A\cos^{\alpha}\theta with θ=ξ/ℓ\theta=\xi/\ell and setting γ=n​α\gamma=n\alpha yields three types of terms:

−c​A​cosα⁡θ+Am​cosm​α⁡θ+Anℓ2​[γ⁡(γ−1)​cosγ−2⁡θ−γ2​cosγ⁡θ]=0.-cA\cos^{\alpha}\theta+A^{m}\cos^{m\alpha}\theta+\frac{A^{n}}{\ell^{2}}\bigl[\gamma(\gamma-1)\cos^{\gamma-2}\theta-\gamma^{2}\cos^{\gamma}\theta\bigr]=0.

Power matching between the translation term (cosα⁡θ\cos^{\alpha}\theta) and the dispersive singular term (cosγ−2⁡θ\cos^{\gamma-2}\theta) forces α=γ−2=n​α−2\alpha=\gamma-2=n\alpha-2, giving α=2/(n−1)\alpha=2/(n-1).

Now the convection term Um=Am​cosm​α⁡θU^{m}=A^{m}\cos^{m\alpha}\theta introduces a power cosm​α⁡θ\cos^{m\alpha}\theta. For the equation to hold identically, this power must coincide with one of the two already present: either m​α=αm\alpha=\alpha (giving m=1m=1, excluded by hypothesis) or m​α=n​αm\alpha=n\alpha (giving m=nm=n).

When m≠nm\neq n (and m>1m>1), the power cosm​α⁡θ\cos^{m\alpha}\theta is linearly independent of both cosα⁡θ\cos^{\alpha}\theta and cosn​α⁡θ\cos^{n\alpha}\theta. Its coefficient AmA^{m} cannot vanish for A>0A>0, so the equation has no solution of cosine-power form. ∎

This proposition explains why the K(m,m) subfamily occupies a distinguished position within the K(m,n) family. The cosine-power profile is the simplest compact traveling wave ansatz, and its restriction to m=nm=n reflects the requirement that the convection and dispersion nonlinearities share the same power structure. For m≠nm\neq n, the mismatch between powers forces the traveling wave profile into elliptic-function or more general transcendental form.

The Rosenau–Zilburg survey [17] presents the broader 𝒞N​(m,a,b)\mathcal{C}_{N}(m,a,b) framework (equations (2.35b)–(2.35d)), which identifies additional cosine-power families when the dispersive term has the generalized structure 1b​[ua​(ub)x​x]x\frac{1}{b}[u^{a}(u^{b})_{xx}]_{x} with a≠0a\neq 0. The K(m,n) equations correspond to a=0a=0, b=nb=n, the most constrained case. Proposition B.1 characterizes the cosine-power solutions within this subfamily completely.

B.2 Phase-plane uniqueness within the symmetric class

The standing hypothesis (H2) in §5.1 assumes that post-collision compactons take the cosine-power form of Theorem 4.1. The following proposition provides partial justification.

Proposition B.2 (Profile uniqueness).

For m>1m>1 and speed c>0c>0, the K(m,m) traveling wave ODE

−c​U+Um+(Um)′′=0-cU+U^{m}+(U^{m})^{\prime\prime}=0 (9)

admits a unique positive, symmetric, single-hump solution with compact support, namely the cosine-power compacton of Theorem 4.1 with amplitude A=(2​m​c/(m+1))1/(m−1)A=(2mc/(m+1))^{1/(m-1)}.

Proof.

The ODE (9) can be written as a first-order system in the phase plane (U,V)(U,V) where V=(Um)′V=(U^{m})^{\prime}. Setting W=UmW=U^{m} and using W′′=−W+c​U=−W+c​W1/mW^{\prime\prime}=-W+cU=-W+cW^{1/m} yields the energy integral

12​(W′)2+Φ⁡(W)=E,\frac{1}{2}(W^{\prime})^{2}+\Phi(W)=E, (59)

where the potential is

Φ⁡(W)=12​W2−c​mm+1​W(m+1)/m.\Phi(W)=\frac{1}{2}W^{2}-\frac{cm}{m+1}W^{(m+1)/m}.

Since W=Um≥0W=U^{m}\geq 0 and UU is positive, we analyze the dynamics of (59) in W≥0W\geq 0.

At W=0W=0, the potential Φ\Phi has a degenerate critical point (with Φ⁡(0)=0\Phi(0)=0 and Φ′​(0)=0\Phi^{\prime}(0)=0). Since Φ\Phi decreases for small W>0W>0 and grows as W2W^{2} for large WW, the level set Φ⁡(W)=0\Phi(W)=0 has a unique positive root at Wturn=[2​m​c/(m+1)]m/(m−1)=AmW_{\mathrm{turn}}=[2mc/(m+1)]^{m/(m-1)}=A^{m}, the compacton peak. For the energy level E=Φ⁡(0)=0E=\Phi(0)=0, the trajectory connects W=0W=0 to WturnW_{\mathrm{turn}} and back, forming a homoclinic orbit in the half-plane W≥0W\geq 0.

Within the class of positive, symmetric, single-hump solutions: (i) symmetry forces W′​(0)=0W^{\prime}(0)=0, so the trajectory reaches WturnW_{\mathrm{turn}} at ξ=0\xi=0; (ii) single-hump means the trajectory does not re-enter the region W′>0W^{\prime}>0 after returning to W′<0W^{\prime}<0; (iii) positivity means W>0W>0 throughout the interior.

Among all energy levels, E=0E=0 is the unique choice satisfying all three conditions: any E>0E>0 prevents the trajectory from reaching W=0W=0 (the orbit becomes periodic), while E<0E<0 is incompatible with W≥0W\geq 0 near the origin. On the E=0E=0 level set, the trajectory is determined uniquely by the energy integral, giving W′​(ξ)=±−2​Φ​(W⁡(ξ))W^{\prime}(\xi)=\pm\sqrt{-2\Phi(W(\xi))} with the sign determined by the direction of traversal. Integration yields the cosine-power profile.

Compact support arises from the degeneracy of Φ\Phi at W=0W=0: near W=0W=0 the potential behaves like −c​mm+1​W(m+1)/m-\frac{cm}{m+1}W^{(m+1)/m}, which vanishes more slowly than quadratically because (m+1)/m<2(m+1)/m<2, so the trajectory reaches W=0W=0 in finite ξ\xi. This is in contrast to the KdV case, where the potential vanishes quadratically and the soliton tail decays exponentially but never reaches zero. ∎

Remark B.3.

Proposition B.2 addresses uniqueness within the class of positive, symmetric, single-hump profiles. The question of whether asymmetric or multi-hump compact traveling waves exist remains open; the phase-plane analysis shows that no such solutions arise on the E=0E=0 energy level, but solutions at E≠0E\neq 0 or with different topology are not excluded. Additionally, for m≥4m\geq 4, the compacton profile has α<1\alpha<1, so U′U^{\prime} diverges at the support boundary. The phase-plane analysis operates in the W=UmW=U^{m} variable, where the boundary behavior is W∼(ξ0−ξ)2​m/(m−1)W\sim(\xi_{0}-\xi)^{2m/(m-1)} near a support edge ξ0\xi_{0}, and all terms remain bounded. Passage back to U=W1/mU=W^{1/m} introduces the fractional-power singularity at the edges.

Appendix D Numerical method

This appendix describes the spectrally-filtered pseudospectral method (PSM) used for the collision simulations in Section 5.1 and for all other K⁡(m,m)K(m,m) computations throughout this paper. The method follows the framework developed in [9], where systematic comparisons across filter variants, dissipation operators, and parameter choices establish the production configuration summarized below.

The filtered equation

We solve the spectrally filtered K(m,m)(m,m) equation in conservative form,

ut+ℱLP​[(um)x+(um)x​x​x]=δ⋅cmax​(t)⋅Δ​x3⋅𝒟⁡[u],u_{t}+\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LP}}\bigl[(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{m})_{xxx}\bigr]=\delta\cdot c_{\max}(t)\cdot\Delta x^{3}\cdot\mathcal{D}[u], (60)

where the low-pass exponential filter ℱLP\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{LP}} is applied jointly to both the advective and dispersive flux terms (Variant C of [9]). This joint filtering eliminates two failure modes: filtering only the advective flux (Variant A) permits spurious growth through the unfiltered dispersive term, while filtering only the dispersive flux (Variant B) is catastrophically unstable for m≥3m\geq 3. Joint filtering avoids both at the cost of a single additional FFT per time step.

The low-pass filter transfer function is

σLP​(k)=exp⁡(−β​(|k|/kc)2​p),kc=kmax/q,\sigma_{\mathrm{LP}}(k)=\exp\!\bigl(-\beta\,(|k|/k_{c})^{2p}\bigr),\qquad k_{c}=k_{\max}/q,

with p=8p=8, fixed cutoff fraction q=2q=2, and β\beta chosen so that σLP​(kmax)=ϵmach\sigma_{\mathrm{LP}}(k_{\max})=\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}. The fixed cutoff q=2q=2 retains modes up to half the Nyquist frequency for all mm; an adaptive cutoff q=mq=m was tested in [9] and found to starve the interior of resolution for m≥3m\geq 3.

Dissipation: biharmonic high-pass with spatial ramp

The dissipation operator 𝒟\mathcal{D} acts through a biharmonic (k4k^{4}) high-pass filter with a smooth spatial ramp that concentrates the dissipation near the compacton boundary,

𝒟⁡[u]=r⁡(x,t)​ℱ−1​[−k4​WHP​(k)​u^​(k)],\mathcal{D}[u]=r(x,t)\,\mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\bigl[-k^{4}\,W_{\mathrm{HP}}(k)\,\hat{u}(k)\bigr],

where WHP​(k)W_{\mathrm{HP}}(k) is a linear ramp from 00 at kck_{c} to 11 at kmaxk_{\max}, and r⁡(x,t)=min⁡(1,uramp/|u⁡(x,t)|)r(x,t)=\min(1,\,u_{\mathrm{ramp}}/|u(x,t)|) with uramp=0.05​maxj​uju_{\mathrm{ramp}}=0.05\,\max_{j}u_{j}. The ramp suppresses dissipation in the compacton interior (where r→0r\to 0) and activates it at the support boundary (where r→1r\to 1), reducing the peak shape error by approximately 47%47\% relative to a sharp-step mask [9].

The amplitude scaling uses the instantaneous maximum wave speed

cmax​(t)=m+12​m​maxj​|uj|m−1,c_{\max}(t)=\frac{m+1}{2m}\,\max_{j}|u_{j}|^{m-1}, (61)

which removes the hidden mm-dependence present in the simpler scaling max⁡|u|m−1\max|u|^{m-1}. A boundary-layer analysis at the compacton edge [9] predicts the universal range δ∈[0.133,0.167]\delta\in[0.133,0.167]; empirical line-search across m∈{2,3,4,5}m\in\{2,3,4,5\} confirms that the single value δ=0.15\delta=0.15 lies within the 1%1\%-insensitivity band for PSM at all mm, requiring no per-equation calibration.

Spatial discretization

Spatial derivatives are computed pseudospectrally: given wavenumbers kj=2​π​j/Lk_{j}=2\pi j/L, the spectral derivative (∂xu)^j=i​kj​u^j\widehat{(\partial_{x}u)}_{j}=ik_{j}\hat{u}_{j} provides machine-precision accuracy for all resolved modes. Third derivatives are obtained by three applications of the spectral derivative. The method is implemented on a uniform periodic grid with NxN_{x} equally spaced points and spacing Δ​x=L/Nx\Delta x=L/N_{x}.

Time integration and grid parameters

We use classical RK4 with fixed timestep satisfying the CFL bound

Δ​t≤C⋅Δ​x3m,\Delta t\leq C\cdot\frac{\Delta x^{3}}{m}, (62)

with safety constant C≈0.8×2.83/4C\approx 0.8\times 2.83/4. All collision simulations use Nx=512N_{x}=512 grid points on the periodic domain [0,L][0,L], exponential LP filter with q=2q=2, biharmonic ramp dissipation with δ=0.15\delta=0.15, and fixed-step RK4 integration. Mass I0I_{0} is conserved to machine precision; energy I1I_{1} is conserved to relative error at most 7.0×10−67.0\times 10^{-6} (Supplement, Table S2). Convergence analysis in [9] confirms rates consistent with the regularity hierarchy: near-second order for m≤3m\leq 3 and regularity-limited floors of order 2/m2/m for m≥4m\geq 4.

Appendix E Weak solution framework

This appendix provides the detailed argument for extending K(m,m) conservation laws to weak solutions, supporting the framework described in §4.2.

For m>3m>3, the compacton profile has α<1\alpha<1 and the classical derivative U′U^{\prime} diverges at the support boundary. The weak formulation (21) transfers all derivatives onto smooth test functions, removing the regularity requirement on uu.

All five conservation laws extend to this weak setting. The conserved integrals remain well-defined and time-independent for solutions satisfying (21), including the fractional-exponent cases where classical derivatives fail. This follows because each conserved density involves at most um+1u^{m+1} and each flux can be reduced, via integration by parts, to integrals of umu^{m} and its weak derivatives, all of which are well-defined for u∈Lm+1∩H−1u\in L^{m+1}\cap H^{-1}.

Compacton collisions for m≥4m\geq 4 involve interactions between solutions whose derivatives diverge at their support boundaries. The conservation-elasticity framework of Theorems 5.1 and 5.5 applies uniformly across the family because the five conservation laws hold in the weak sense for all m≥2m\geq 2.

Anco and Gandarias [2] subsequently developed a rigorous distributional framework establishing that weak compacton solutions satisfy the associated continuity equations in a well-defined distributional sense, even at the support boundary where classical derivatives may not exist.

Appendix F Conservation law derivations

This appendix provides detailed proofs and evaluations for the five K(m,m) conservation laws stated in §4.3.

F.1 Verification of trigonometric conservation

To verify conservation of I2I_{2}, note that

d​I2d​t=−∫[(um)x+(um)x​x​x]sin(x)dx.\frac{dI_{2}}{dt}=-\int\bigl[(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{m})_{xxx}\bigr]\sin(x)\,dx.

Integrating the convection term by parts once gives ∫um​cos⁡(x)​𝑑x\int u^{m}\cos(x)\,dx. Integrating the dispersion term by parts three times gives −∫umcos(x)dx-\int u^{m}\cos(x)\,dx (each integration alternates the trigonometric function, and the third produces the required sign reversal). The two contributions cancel exactly, giving d​I2/d​t=0dI_{2}/dt=0. An identical argument with cos⁡(x)\cos(x) replacing sin⁡(x)\sin(x) establishes d​I3/d​t=0dI_{3}/dt=0.

This cancellation is specific to wavenumber k=1k=1. For test functions sin⁡(k​x)\sin(kx) and cos⁡(k​x)\cos(kx) with k≠1k\neq 1, the convection and dispersion terms produce kk and k3k^{3} respectively, which fail to cancel.

F.2 Conservation of nonlocal momentum

Conservation of the nonlocal momentum I4I_{4} follows from the factorization of the Hamiltonian operator. Define v=(Dx2+1)−1​[u]v=(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1}[u], so that v+vx​x=uv+v_{xx}=u and consequently vx+vx​x​x=uxv_{x}+v_{xxx}=u_{x}. (The pseudoinverse is well-defined because compacton solutions satisfy u^​(±1)=0\hat{u}(\pm 1)=0, placing uu in the range of Dx2+1D_{x}^{2}+1.) By the self-adjointness of (Dx2+1)−1(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1},

d​I4d​t=2∫ut⋅vdx=−2∫[(um)x+(um)x​x​x]vdx.\frac{dI_{4}}{dt}=2\int u_{t}\cdot v\,dx=-2\int\bigl[(u^{m})_{x}+(u^{m})_{xxx}\bigr]v\,dx.

Integrating by parts (once and three times, respectively) gives

=2​∫um​(vx+vx​x​x)​𝑑x=2​∫um​ux​𝑑x=0,=2\int u^{m}\bigl(v_{x}+v_{xxx}\bigr)dx=2\int u^{m}\,u_{x}\,dx=0,

where the last step uses the total derivative identity

∫um​ux​𝑑x=∫1m+1​(um+1)x​𝑑x=0.\int u^{m}u_{x}\,dx=\int\frac{1}{m+1}(u^{m+1})_{x}\,dx=0.

The key identity vx+vx​x​x=uxv_{x}+v_{xxx}=u_{x} holds precisely because (Dx2+1)−1(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1} commutes with DxD_{x}; this in turn reflects the factorization 𝔇=−(Dx3+Dx)=−Dx​(Dx2+1)\mathfrak{D}=-(D_{x}^{3}+D_{x})=-D_{x}(D_{x}^{2}+1) of the Hamiltonian operator. The cancellation that produces d​I4/d​t=0dI_{4}/dt=0 requires m=nm=n: for general K(m,n), the computation yields 2​∫(um−un)​vx​𝑑x2\int(u^{m}-u^{n})v_{x}\,dx, which does not vanish when m≠nm\neq n.

F.3 Casimir structure: why four local laws

Three of the four local laws are Casimir functionals of the Hamiltonian operator 𝔇=−(Dx3+Dx)\mathfrak{D}=-(D_{x}^{3}+D_{x}): they are conserved for any evolution equation of the form ut=𝔇⁡(f)u_{t}=\mathfrak{D}(f), regardless of the choice of ff. A functional 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a Casimir of 𝔇\mathfrak{D} if 𝔇⁡(δ​𝒞/δ​u)=0\mathfrak{D}(\delta\mathcal{C}/\delta u)=0, i.e., its variational derivative lies in ker⁡(𝔇)\ker(\mathfrak{D}). The kernel of 𝔇=−(Dx3+Dx)\mathfrak{D}=-(D_{x}^{3}+D_{x}) consists of solutions to γx​x​x+γx=0\gamma_{xxx}+\gamma_{x}=0, which has the three-dimensional solution space {1,cos⁡x,sin⁡x}\{1,\,\cos x,\,\sin x\}. These yield mass (I0I_{0}, from γ=1\gamma=1) and the two trigonometric laws (I2I_{2} and I3I_{3}, from γ=sin⁡x\gamma=\sin x and cos⁡x\cos x). No other Casimirs exist.

The fourth local law, energy (I1I_{1}), is the one conservation law specific to K(m,m): it is the Hamiltonian functional itself, ℋ=∫um+1/(m+1)​𝑑x\mathcal{H}=\int u^{m+1}/(m+1)\,dx, whose conservation follows from the antisymmetry of 𝔇\mathfrak{D}. It is associated through Noether’s theorem with time-translation invariance. The absence of a recursion operator prevents this single dynamical conservation law from generating further ones.

The nonlocal law I4I_{4} arises from the factorization 𝔇=−Dx​(Dx2+1)\mathfrak{D}=-D_{x}(D_{x}^{2}+1). Its density involves the inverse operator (Dx2+1)−1(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1}, placing it outside the local framework. Conservation of I4I_{4} requires m=nm=n and thus reflects the specific algebraic structure of K(m,m).

F.4 Evaluated conservation integrals

For a single compacton with amplitude AA, the four local conservation integrals evaluate explicitly through Beta functions. Using the universal formulas α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1) and ℓ=2​m/(m−1)\ell=2m/(m-1):

I0\displaystyle I_{0} =A​ℓ⋅B⁡(α+12,12),\displaystyle=A\ell\cdot B\!\left(\tfrac{\alpha+1}{2},\,\tfrac{1}{2}\right), (63)
I1\displaystyle I_{1} =Am+1​ℓm+1⋅B⁡((m+1)​α+12,12).\displaystyle=\frac{A^{m+1}\ell}{m+1}\cdot B\!\left(\tfrac{(m+1)\alpha+1}{2},\,\tfrac{1}{2}\right). (64)

For K(2,2): I0=2​π​AI_{0}=2\pi A, I1=(5​π/12)​A3I_{1}=(5\pi/12)A^{3}. For K(3,3): I0=6​AI_{0}=6A, I1=(9​π/32)​A4I_{1}=(9\pi/32)A^{4}. The shift from transcendental (π\pi-dependent) to rational mass coefficients at m=3m=3 mirrors the regularity transition: cusped edges produce simpler mass integrals than smooth ones, though the energy retains π\pi-dependence in both cases.

The trigonometric integrals I2I_{2} and I3I_{3} depend on compacton position as well as amplitude, encoding spatial phase information. The nonlocal momentum I4I_{4} has a closed form on compactons: since (Dx2+1)−1​U=Um/c(D_{x}^{2}+1)^{-1}U=U^{m}/c, it equals (m+1)​I1/c(m+1)I_{1}/c, which scales as A2A^{2}; for K(2,2), I4=(5​π/3)​A2I_{4}=(5\pi/3)A^{2} and for K(3,3), I4=(27​π/16)​A2I_{4}=(27\pi/16)A^{2}. This agrees with the scaling I4∼A2​ℓI_{4}\sim A^{2}\ell verified computationally for m=2,…,7m=2,\ldots,7 using both Maple and Mathematica.

Appendix G Hamiltonian and Casimir analysis

This appendix provides the detailed bi-Hamiltonian obstruction analysis summarized in §4.4.

G.1 The KdV bi-Hamiltonian structure

KdV possesses two compatible Hamiltonian structures: a first-order operator 𝒥1=−∂x\mathcal{J}_{1}=-\partial_{x} and a third-order operator 𝒥2=−∂x​x​x−23(u∂x+∂x⋅u)\mathcal{J}_{2}=-\partial_{xxx}-\frac{2}{3}(u\,\partial_{x}+\partial_{x}\!\cdot\,u). The compatibility condition (that every linear combination a​𝒥1+b​𝒥2a\mathcal{J}_{1}+b\mathcal{J}_{2} is again a Poisson operator [29]) produces the recursion operator ℛ=𝒥2​𝒥1−1\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{J}_{2}\,\mathcal{J}_{1}^{-1}, which generates the infinite conservation hierarchy: applying ℛ\mathcal{R} to the gradient of one conserved functional produces the gradient of the next. The Lenard recursion scheme converts bi-Hamiltonian structure into an algebraic machine for manufacturing conservation laws [12].

G.2 Why K(m,m) admits no compatible second operator

The K(m,m) Hamiltonian operator 𝔇=−(Dx3+Dx)\mathfrak{D}=-(D_{x}^{3}+D_{x}) has constant coefficients. Systematic searches for a second Poisson operator compatible with 𝔇\mathfrak{D} fail for all m≥2m\geq 2. This failure is intimately connected to Vodová’s symmetry analysis: a compatible second operator would induce a recursion operator generating symmetries of arbitrarily high order, contradicting Proposition 2 of [46], which establishes that no generalized symmetries of order greater than 33 exist. The nonlinear dispersion term (um)x​x​x(u^{m})_{xxx} is the root cause: it prevents the construction of uu-dependent Poisson operators that could serve as bi-Hamiltonian partners.

G.3 Three consequences of the obstruction

The absence of a second compatible Poisson structure has three concrete consequences for K(m,m):

  1. 1.

    No recursion operator. Without a compatible pair, the Lenard recursion scheme cannot operate. This explains the termination of the hierarchy at five laws (Theorem 4.6).

  2. 2.

    Vacuous involutivity. In bi-Hamiltonian systems the generated conservation laws are automatically in involution and each generates a distinct flow. For K(m,m) the five laws are in involution under (30) (three are Casimirs and {ℋ,I4}=0\{\mathcal{H},I_{4}\}=0), but only two commuting flows result, time evolution and translation.

  3. 3.

    No action-angle variables. Complete integrability in the Liouville sense requires sufficiently many conserved quantities in involution to fill out the phase space. With only these two commuting flows, the reduction to action-angle coordinates that makes integrable systems explicitly solvable is unavailable [3].

Appendix H Collision data and detailed numerics

This appendix provides detailed numerical methodology and additional results supporting the collision analysis in §5.1.

H.1 Alternative elasticity measures

Several natural alternatives to the amplitude-sum elasticity (31) exist. An energy-based measure uses the Hamiltonian energy integral:

ℰE=E1′+E2′E1+E2,where ​Ei=Dm​Aim+1,\mathcal{E}_{E}\;=\;\frac{E^{\prime}_{1}+E^{\prime}_{2}}{E_{1}+E_{2}},\qquad\text{where }E_{i}=D_{m}\,A_{i}^{m+1}, (65)

with Dm=ℓm+1​B​((m+1)​α+12,12)D_{m}=\frac{\ell}{m+1}\,B\bigl(\frac{(m+1)\alpha+1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\bigr) the energy integral coefficient of (64). An L2L^{2}-based measure replaces the energy by squared norms:

ℰ2=‖u1′‖22+‖u2′‖22‖u1‖22+‖u2‖22.\mathcal{E}_{2}\;=\;\frac{\|u^{\prime}_{1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|u^{\prime}_{2}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|u_{1}\|_{2}^{2}+\|u_{2}\|_{2}^{2}}. (66)

For K(m,m) compactons, Theorem 4.1 yields Ei∝Aim+1E_{i}\propto A_{i}^{m+1} and ‖ui‖22∝Ai2​α+1​ℓ\|u_{i}\|_{2}^{2}\propto A_{i}^{2\alpha+1}\ell, so each alternative measure is a monotone function of the amplitude ratio. Writing Ai′=(1−ϵi)​AiA^{\prime}_{i}=(1-\epsilon_{i})A_{i} with small ϵi\epsilon_{i}, one finds ℰE≈1−(m+1)​ϵ¯\mathcal{E}_{E}\approx 1-(m+1)\bar{\epsilon} and ℰ2≈1−(2​α+1)​ϵ¯\mathcal{E}_{2}\approx 1-(2\alpha+1)\bar{\epsilon}, where ϵ¯\bar{\epsilon} is the weighted mean amplitude deficit. Since m+1>1m+1>1 and 2​α+1>12\alpha+1>1 for all m>1m>1, both alternative measures register a larger departure from unity than ℰ\mathcal{E} itself, but the ordering across different values of mm is preserved. The monotonicity claim in Conjecture 5.7 is therefore invariant under any elasticity measure that depends monotonically on the amplitude ratio.

H.2 Debris extraction methodology

Post-collision integration times are computed dynamically to ensure full compacton separation before debris extraction. Debris is defined as the residual field after subtracting Nelder–Mead least-squares fits of compacton profiles to the two emergent structures. Spectral analysis is restricted to wavenumbers below the filter cutoff κcut=2​π​⌈Nx/(2​q)⌉/L\kappa_{\mathrm{cut}}=2\pi\lceil N_{x}/(2q)\rceil/L, where the solver’s physical dynamics are well resolved; above κcut\kappa_{\mathrm{cut}}, the low-pass filter zeros the advection term and residual content is numerical rather than physical. Signal-to-noise ratios are established by comparing collision debris spectra against single-compacton propagation controls run with identical parameters.

H.3 Extended multi-mm validation

The debris energy fraction ranges from 3.7×10−53.7\times 10^{-5} at m=2m=2 to 1.5×10−61.5\times 10^{-6} at m=5m=5, remaining below 4×10−54\times 10^{-5} across all cases. The spectral peak shift from kpeak≈0.38k_{\mathrm{peak}}\approx 0.38 to kpeak≈3.6k_{\mathrm{peak}}\approx 3.6 reflects the narrowing compacton half-width as mm increases (from π​ℓ/2≈6.28\pi\ell/2\approx 6.28 at m=2m=2 to π​ℓ/2≈3.93\pi\ell/2\approx 3.93 at m=5m=5): sharper compacton profiles generate shorter-wavelength debris upon collision. Grid convergence tests from Nx=256N_{x}=256 through Nx=1024N_{x}=1024 confirm that the notch deepens with refinement while the debris spectrum stabilizes.

Appendix I BBM comparison: extended results

This appendix provides the detailed BBM collision simulation methodology and extended results supporting the landscape analysis in §5.2.

I.1 BBM simulation methodology

We solve the BBM equation in the Fourier-transformed form

ut=−(1−∂x​x)−1∂x(u+12u2),u_{t}=-\bigl(1-\partial_{xx}\bigr)^{-1}\partial_{x}\bigl(u+\tfrac{1}{2}u^{2}\bigr), (67)

where the operator (1−∂x​x)−1∂x(1-\partial_{xx})^{-1}\partial_{x} has Fourier symbol −ik/(1+k2)-ik/(1+k^{2}), converting the implicit time derivative into an explicit ODE. The pseudospectral discretization uses Nx=4096N_{x}=4096 grid points on a periodic domain with two-thirds dealiasing and RK45 time stepping (rtol=10−8\texttt{rtol}=10^{-8}, atol=10−10\texttt{atol}=10^{-10}). Validation against the exact single-soliton solution u⁡(x,t)=A​sech2⁡(κ⁡(x−c​t))u(x,t)=A\operatorname{sech}^{2}\bigl(\kappa(x-ct)\bigr) with c=1+A/3c=1+A/3 and κ=(c−1)/(4​c)\kappa=\sqrt{(c-1)/(4c)} confirms propagation errors below 2×10−72\times 10^{-7}, conservation of mass to 10−810^{-8}–10−910^{-9}, and conservation of the L2L^{2} norm to 10−610^{-6}–10−710^{-7}.

Two-soliton collisions were performed across a range of amplitudes (A1=0.5A_{1}=0.5 to 2020) and amplitude ratios (r=A2/A1=0.1r=A_{2}/A_{1}=0.1 to 0.90.9), with the faster soliton overtaking the slower. Post-collision amplitudes were extracted by peak detection after the solitons separated cleanly.

I.2 Extended landscape discussion

Three additional observations refine the landscape picture. First, the entries at N=2N=2 and N=1N=1 in the landscape table represent expectations based on general arguments rather than systematic numerical studies. Second, whether the algebraic structure of the conservation laws matters, and not merely their number, is open: laws that generate independent commuting flows (as in near-integrable systems) may contribute more to elasticity than Casimirs, which generate none. Third, the odd-even asymmetry in collision robustness discovered by Garralón-López et al. [14] provides independent evidence for finer structure: although all K(pp,pp) equations share N=5N=5, the algebraic form of the laws varies with pp, and collision outcomes differ accordingly.

Appendix J Periodic wave calculations

This appendix collects the detailed periodic wave analysis for K(2,2) shelf waves, supporting the summary in §7.3.

J.1 Period formula and quadrature

The small-amplitude oscillation period at the center equilibrium v0=a2v_{0}=a^{2} is

T0=2​π1−c/(2​a),T_{0}=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{1-c/(2a)}}\,, (68)

which diverges as c→(2​a)−c\to(2a)^{-}. At intermediate energies, the period is given by

T⁡(E)=2​∫vmin​(E)vmax​(E)d​v2​(E−V​(v)),T(E)=2\int_{v_{\min}(E)}^{v_{\max}(E)}\frac{dv}{\sqrt{2(E-V(v))}}\,, (69)

where VV is given by the K(2,2) potential (42).

J.2 Elliptic structure

Because VV involves v3/2v^{3/2} rather than a polynomial in vv, the resulting cnoidal wave profiles are not standard Jacobi elliptic functions. In the ww-variable, where the first integral (compare (46)) is a polynomial P4​(w)P_{4}(w) of degree four, the curve y2=P4​(w)y^{2}=P_{4}(w) has genus one, so the profiles are given implicitly by elliptic integrals. The differential w​d​w/yw\,dw/y that defines ξ\xi is of the second kind, which is why the profile is not a Jacobi cn2\mathrm{cn}^{2} as it is for KdV.

Appendix K Open problems

Eight open problems arise from this investigation. Each is stated concisely below; extended versions with detailed research programs and methodological discussion appear in the Supplement, §S7.

Problem 1. Uniqueness of the cosine-power profile. Theorem 4.1 derives the universal formulas from the cosine-power ansatz; Proposition B.2 establishes uniqueness among positive, symmetric, single-hump solutions. The full question (whether every compact-support traveling wave of K(m,m) at prescribed speed takes the cosine-power form without symmetry assumptions) remains open. Phase-plane analysis excludes alternatives on the zero-energy level set, but other energy levels have not been ruled out.

Problem 2. Within-class monotonicity and cross-class geometry. BBM solitary waves (N=3N=3, smooth tails) and K(m,m) compactons (N=5N=5, compact support) collide comparably elastically by the amplitude measure, while K(m,m) sheds less debris energy, so the comparison does not separate conservation count from interaction geometry. Conjecture 5.7 posits monotonicity within each geometric class, with interaction geometry as a possible independent modulating factor. Systematic testing across multiple equation families with different conservation counts and tail behaviors would convert this into a precise scaling law.

Problem 3. Stability theory for fractional-exponent compactons. The translation generator PP increases along the compacton family (Corollary 4.5), but the Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss framework does not apply to K(m,m) for any m>1m>1, because the second variation of ℋ−c​P\mathcal{H}-cP has infinitely many negative directions. A stability theory for compactons needs a different mechanism. For m>3m>3 (Hölder regularity C0,αC^{0,\alpha} with α<1\alpha<1), extending stability theory to weighted Sobolev or Besov spaces is needed. The cusp case m=3m=3 (codimension-one transition) may be the most tractable starting point, and the singular limit a→0+a\to 0^{+} of smooth shelf-wave stability provides a regularization pathway.

Problem 4. Interaction geometry and collision elasticity. Can interaction geometry be quantified through a single parameter (tail decay rate κ\kappa or regularity exponent α\alpha) that correlates predictably with collision elasticity at fixed conservation count? The K(m,m) family provides a testing ground (α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1) varies while N=5N=5 is fixed), and the shelf-wave family offers tunable κ\kappa within a single equation.

Problem 5. Master formulas for the full K(m,n) family. Proposition B.1 shows the cosine-power ansatz is exclusive to the diagonal n=mn=m. Whether unified two-parameter formulas α⁡(m,n)\alpha(m,n), ℓ⁡(m,n)\ell(m,n), c⁡(m,n,A)c(m,n,A) exist for off-diagonal K(m,n) compactons remains open, as does the square-wave limit m→∞m\to\infty (§4.2), where α→0+\alpha\to 0^{+}.

Problem 6. Approximate integrability frameworks. Hernández Heredero et al. rule out exact Lax pairs for K(m,m) with m>1m>1, but approximate analogues are not excluded. Promising directions include asymptotic Lax-operator deformation from KdV toward K(2,2) and data-driven discovery of approximate conservation laws via physics-informed neural networks.

Problem 7. Experimental observation of compactons. No controlled laboratory observation of compacton propagation and collision has been achieved. Granular chains with Hertzian contacts and nonlinear optical media with engineered dispersion are the leading candidate platforms.

Problem 8. Multi-compacton collision asymptotics. Pairwise collisions are quasi-elastic; the long-time behavior of NN-compacton initial data (whether debris accumulates or dynamics remains dominated by coherent structures) is unknown. Simultaneous three-body collisions have not been studied systematically.

Computational Supplement to:
What Remains When Integrability Fails?
Mathematical Structure in the K(m,m) Compacton Equations

S1 Overview and Relationship to Main Paper

This document collects computational material supporting the main paper. All collision simulations in the main text use the spectrally-filtered pseudospectral method (PSM) described in Appendix D of the main paper, with parameters Nx=512N_{x}=512 grid points, exponential low-pass filter with cutoff q=2q=2, biharmonic ramp dissipation with δ=0.15\delta=0.15, and fixed-step classical RK4 time integration. The runs of Table S2, which underlie Table  and Figure  of the main paper, and the collision of its Figure  use a periodic domain with L=100L=100 and grid spacing Δ​x=L/N≈0.195\Delta x=L/N\approx 0.195; the two collisions quoted in Section  of the main paper use [0,200][0,200].

The K(mm,mm) collision data (Section S2) supports Section 5 of the main paper; the BBM comparison data (Section S3) supports the landscape analysis. Post-collision amplitudes are extracted by Nelder–Mead least-squares fitting of compacton profiles. Debris spectral analysis is restricted to wavenumbers below the filter cutoff κcut=2​π​⌈Nx/(2​q)⌉/L≈8.04\kappa_{\mathrm{cut}}=2\pi\lceil N_{x}/(2q)\rceil/L\approx 8.04 rad/unit length.

S2 Complete K(m,m) Collision Dataset

Table S2 reports the complete collision measurements for K(mm,mm) with m=2,3,4,5m=2,3,4,5, pre-collision amplitudes A1=1.0A_{1}=1.0, A2=0.5A_{2}=0.5 (ratio r=0.5r=0.5), and Nx=512N_{x}=512 grid points. These are the data underlying Table  and Figure  of the main paper.

Debris assessment.

The spectrally-filtered pseudospectral method produces debris energy fractions ranging from 3.7×10−53.7\times 10^{-5} at m=2m=2 to 1.5×10−61.5\times 10^{-6} at m=5m=5, all well below the levels reported for the earlier finite-difference scheme [9]. The spectral notch near k=1k=1 is clearly visible for all values of mm, with notch ratios below 0.030.03, confirming the prediction of the constraint-deficit mechanism (Theorem (c)).

S3 BBM Comparison Dataset

Tables S3, S4, and S5 report the complete BBM collision measurements supporting the landscape analysis in Section 5 of the main paper.

Method.

The BBM equation is solved in Fourier-transformed form ut=−(1−∂x​x)−1∂x(u+12u2)u_{t}=-(1-\partial_{xx})^{-1}\partial_{x}(u+\tfrac{1}{2}u^{2}) with pseudospectral discretization (Nx=4096N_{x}=4096 grid points, two-thirds dealiasing, RK45 with rtol=10−8\texttt{rtol}=10^{-8}, atol=10−10\texttt{atol}=10^{-10}). Validation: single-soliton propagation error 1.48×10−71.48\times 10^{-7}; mass conservation ∼10−8\sim 10^{-8}–10−910^{-9}; L2L^{2} conservation ∼10−6\sim 10^{-6}–10−710^{-7}.

Summary statistics.

Across the 16 rows of Tables S3–S5 (14 distinct configurations: (A1,A2)=(2,1)(A_{1},A_{2})=(2,1) appears in Tables S3 and S4, and (10,5)(10,5) in Tables S3 and S5, each time with identical values), the BBM amplitude elasticity ranges from ℰ=0.9993\mathcal{E}=0.9993 to 1.00011.0001, with a typical value of 0.9997±0.00020.9997\pm 0.0002 (mean and standard deviation over the 14 distinct configurations). Debris energy fractions range from 10−510^{-5} to 6×10−46\times 10^{-4}. The near-unit elasticity ℰ>1\mathcal{E}>1 observed at (A1,A2)=(6.0,3.0)(A_{1},A_{2})=(6.0,3.0) is within the measurement uncertainty of the peak-detection method and does not indicate energy creation; it likely reflects a small bias in the post-collision amplitude extraction.

S4 Additional Computational Investigations

This section describes supplementary numerical experiments that extend the main paper’s results.

S4.1 Compacton emergence: extended data

The main paper’s Section  establishes compacton emergence from a wide-compacton initial pulse for the K(m,m)(m,m) family (m=2,3,4,5m=2,3,4,5) and the mixed cases K(2,3)(2,3) and K(3,2)(3,2). This subsection provides three pieces of supplementary evidence: a direct propagation-speed validation table, the sub-threshold trailing-peak amplitudes that fall below the genuine-compacton cutoff in the main paper’s table, and a complementary experiment using Gaussian rather than wide-compacton initial data.

Direct propagation-speed validation.

The implications statement in Section  references a direct measurement of the leading-compacton propagation speed. The full validation data are reported in Table S6. Peak positions were tracked across four snapshots at t=100,125,150,175t=100,125,150,175, and the propagation speed was extracted by linear regression of peak position versus time for each detected compacton. The measured speed is then compared to the exact traveling-wave prediction cpred=[(n+1)/(m+n)]​Am−1c_{\mathrm{pred}}=[(n+1)/(m+n)]\,A^{m-1} (evaluated with the mean amplitude across snapshots), which reduces to the universal formula [(m+1)/(2​m)]​Am−1[(m+1)/(2m)]\,A^{m-1} for K(m,m)(m,m).

Sub-threshold trailing peaks.

The main paper reports trailing compactons with amplitude above the genuine-compacton threshold of 0.080.08. The peak detector also identifies fainter structures below this threshold that the authors consider unresolved at the present spectral resolution. For completeness, the K(3,3)(3,3) run detected a fourth peak at A4≈0.10A_{4}\approx 0.10, just above the threshold; it is not cleanly separable from numerical noise and is reported in the main table as marginal, marked with a dagger. K(4,4)(4,4) and K(5,5)(5,5) produced no detectable fourth structure. Whether these are physical compactons that would be resolved at higher NxN_{x}, or numerical artifacts at the current resolution, requires a refinement study deferred to future work.

Gaussian initial data: complementary experiment.

The main paper’s emergence experiment uses a stretched wide-compacton profile as initial data. As a complementary test of robustness, we also evolved K(2,2) from a Gaussian pulse u(x,0)=A0exp(−x2/σ2)u(x,0)=A_{0}\exp(-x^{2}/\sigma^{2}) for several values of A0A_{0} and σ\sigma. In every case tested (A0=0.5A_{0}=0.5–2.02.0, σ=3\sigma=3–1010), the solution resolves into a finite train of compactons ordered by amplitude, plus a dispersive debris tail. The emergent compacton amplitudes and widths match the universal formulas of Theorem  in the main paper to within 0.5%0.5\%, providing additional evidence that the cosine-power profile acts as an attracting structure for the K(2,2) evolution. The number of emergent compactons increases with the L1L^{1} norm of the initial data, suggestive of a mass-partitioning mechanism loosely analogous to the KdV initial-value resolution into solitons.

S5 Numerical Method: Detailed Description

This section provides additional detail on the spectrally-filtered pseudospectral method (PSM) summarized in Appendix D of the main paper. The full systematic development, including comparisons across filter variants, dissipation operators, and parameter calibration, appears in [9].

S5.1 Motivation for spectral filtering

The compact support of K(m,n)(m,n) compactons poses a fundamental challenge for numerical simulation. Standard spectral methods suffer from Gibbs oscillations at the support boundary, where the solution transitions abruptly from a smooth profile to zero. These oscillations amplify through the nonlinear terms and typically cause numerical instability within a few time units. The spectrally-filtered approach described here eliminates this difficulty while preserving the essential structure of the equation.

S5.2 Joint low-pass filtering (Variant C)

The nonlinear terms (um)x(u^{m})_{x} and (um)x​x​x(u^{m})_{xxx} generate high-frequency components through aliasing: if uu contains modes up to wavenumber kmaxk_{\max}, then umu^{m} contains modes up to m⋅kmaxm\cdot k_{\max}. These aliased components corrupt the solution and seed instabilities. Applying an exponential low-pass filter

σLP​(k)=exp⁡(−β​(|k|/kc)2​p),kc=kmax/q,\sigma_{\mathrm{LP}}(k)=\exp\!\bigl(-\beta\,(|k|/k_{c})^{2p}\bigr),\qquad k_{c}=k_{\max}/q,

with p=8p=8 and fixed cutoff q=2q=2 jointly to both flux terms (Variant C of [9]) removes the aliased content while preserving the physically relevant low-frequency dynamics. The constant β\beta is chosen so that σLP​(kmax)=ϵmach\sigma_{\mathrm{LP}}(k_{\max})=\epsilon_{\mathrm{mach}}.

Three filter variants were tested systematically in [9]: Variant A (LP on advection only), Variant B (LP on dispersion only), and Variant C (joint LP on both). Variant B is catastrophically unstable for m≥3m\geq 3, and Variant A permits spurious growth through the unfiltered dispersive term. Variant C avoids both failure modes at the cost of a single additional FFT per time step and is adopted for all simulations in this paper.

The fixed cutoff q=2q=2 retains modes up to half the Nyquist frequency for all mm. An adaptive cutoff q=mq=m was tested and found to starve the interior of resolution for m≥3m\geq 3, degrading convergence rates.

S5.3 Biharmonic high-pass dissipation with spatial ramp

The right-hand side of the filtered equation introduces artificial dissipation to damp the high-frequency oscillations that spectral differentiation generates at the compact support boundary. The dissipation operator 𝒟\mathcal{D} uses a biharmonic (k4k^{4}) transfer function with a linear ramp in the high-pass band,

𝒟⁡[u]=r⁡(x,t)​ℱ−1​[−k4​WHP​(k)​u^​(k)],\mathcal{D}[u]=r(x,t)\,\mathcal{F}^{-1}\!\bigl[-k^{4}\,W_{\mathrm{HP}}(k)\,\hat{u}(k)\bigr],

where WHP​(k)W_{\mathrm{HP}}(k) ramps linearly from 00 at kck_{c} to 11 at kmaxk_{\max}, and r⁡(x,t)=min⁡(1,uramp/|u⁡(x,t)|)r(x,t)=\min(1,\,u_{\mathrm{ramp}}/|u(x,t)|) is a smooth spatial ramp with uramp=0.05​maxj​uju_{\mathrm{ramp}}=0.05\,\max_{j}u_{j}. This concentrates dissipation near the compacton boundary while suppressing it in the interior, reducing the peak shape error by approximately 47%47\% relative to a sharp-step mask [9].

The scaling factor uses the instantaneous maximum wave speed cmax​(t)=m+12​m​maxj​|uj|m−1c_{\max}(t)=\tfrac{m+1}{2m}\max_{j}|u_{j}|^{m-1}, which removes the hidden mm-dependence present in the simpler scaling max⁡|u|m−1\max|u|^{m-1}. Combined with the explicit Δ​x3\Delta x^{3} factor, the dissipation term vanishes in the limit Δ​x→0\Delta x\to 0, guaranteeing convergence to the unfiltered equation under mesh refinement.

A boundary-layer analysis at the compacton edge [9] predicts the universal range δ∈[0.133,0.167]\delta\in[0.133,0.167]; empirical line-search across m∈{2,3,4,5}m\in\{2,3,4,5\} confirms that δ=0.15\delta=0.15 lies within the 1%1\%-insensitivity band for all tested values of mm.

S5.4 Pseudospectral spatial discretization

Spatial derivatives are computed pseudospectrally: given wavenumbers kj=2​π​j/Lk_{j}=2\pi j/L, the spectral derivative (∂xu)^j=i​kj​u^j\widehat{(\partial_{x}u)}_{j}=ik_{j}\hat{u}_{j} provides machine-precision accuracy for all resolved modes. Third derivatives are obtained by three applications of the spectral derivative. This approach was validated in [9] against a fourth-order finite-difference method (FDM4), with both producing statistically equivalent collision results.

S5.5 Time integration details

Fixed-step integration was adopted after systematic comparison with adaptive Runge–Kutta–Fehlberg (RK45) methods: for a given error tolerance, fixed-step RK4 is roughly 1.4×1.4\times faster because error-estimation overhead exceeds the savings from occasional larger steps in this uniformly stiff problem.

S5.6 Validation and convergence

We validate the numerical scheme through the following diagnostics:

  1. 1.

    Conservation law monitoring: The mass I0=∫u​𝑑xI_{0}=\int u\,dx is conserved to machine precision (relative error at most 1.5×10−151.5\times 10^{-15}, Table S2) by the pseudospectral discretization. The energy I1=∫um+1m+1​𝑑xI_{1}=\int\tfrac{u^{m+1}}{m+1}\,dx, which is not automatically preserved by discretization, provides the meaningful diagnostic: it is conserved to relative error at most 7.0×10−67.0\times 10^{-6} (Table S2).

  2. 2.

    Amplitude preservation: For a single compacton propagating without collision, the peak amplitude changes by less than 0.02%0.02\% over t=100t=100 time units for all values of mm tested.

  3. 3.

    Grid convergence: Convergence analysis in [9] confirms rates consistent with the regularity hierarchy: near-second order for m≤3m\leq 3 and regularity-limited floors of order 2/m2/m for m≥4m\geq 4.

  4. 4.

    Amplitude scaling: Debris energy increases monotonically with collision strength (amplitude ratio A2/A1A_{2}/A_{1} from 0.250.25 to 0.750.75), confirming physical rather than numerical origin.

S6 Painlevé test: detailed expansion

This section provides the complete Painlevé analysis of the K(m,m) traveling wave ODE, summarized in Main Paper §(c) of the main paper.

For K(m,m) with m>1m>1, dominant balance analysis of the traveling wave ODE near movable singularities [1] reveals that solutions behave as

u∼a0(z−z0)−2/(m−1)u\sim a_{0}(z-z_{0})^{-2/(m-1)} (1)

in the complex plane, where z0z_{0} is the singularity location. The exponent −2/(m−1)-2/(m-1) is the negative dual of the compacton’s edge exponent +2/(m−1)+2/(m-1): the same algebraic structure that produces compact support in real solutions generates movable singularities in the complex domain.

The quantity 2/(m−1)2/(m-1) is a positive integer only when m−1m-1 divides 22, restricting attention to m=2m=2 (giving a double pole, u∼a0​(z−z0)−2u\sim a_{0}(z-z_{0})^{-2}) and m=3m=3 (giving a simple pole, u∼a0​(z−z0)−1u\sim a_{0}(z-z_{0})^{-1}).

The case m=2m=2.

The leading singularity is a double pole. Substituting a Laurent series u=∑k=0∞ak​(z−z0)k−2u=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k}(z-z_{0})^{k-2} into the K(2,2) traveling wave ODE and matching powers determines the resonance structure. The resonances (values of kk where aka_{k} is free) must occur at non-negative integers for the Painlevé property to hold. For K(2,2), the resonances occur at k=−1k=-1 and k=6k=6: the value k=−1k=-1 is the universal Fuchs index, and k=6k=6 is the non-trivial resonance where a6a_{6} should be free. Subsequent compatibility conditions at higher order fail: the system requires aka_{k} to satisfy contradictory constraints, introducing logarithmic branch cuts of the form (z−z0)k​log⁡(z−z0)(z-z_{0})^{k}\log(z-z_{0}). These logarithmic terms violate the Painlevé property.

Generic m>1m>1 with m≠2,3m\neq 2,3.

For all other values, including the entire interval 1<m<21<m<2 where 2/(m−1)>22/(m-1)>2 is generically irrational, the leading exponent −2/(m−1)-2/(m-1) is itself non-integer. Branch points appear at the first level of the expansion: the solution near the singularity involves fractional powers (z−z0)−2/(m−1)(z-z_{0})^{-2/(m-1)} that cannot be rewritten as poles. No Laurent series expansion exists, and the Painlevé property fails at the leading order.

The case m=3m=3.

The leading singularity is a simple pole (u∼a0/(z−z0)u\sim a_{0}/(z-z_{0})). While this is the most favorable case, the resonance conditions at higher order again produce incompatibilities, generating movable logarithmic singularities as in the m=2m=2 case.

In summary, movable branch points violate the Painlevé property for every K(m,m) equation with m>1m>1. The failure is structural rather than incidental: it reflects the power-law nonlinearity in the dispersive term (um)x​x​x(u^{m})_{xxx}, which generates non-integer exponents in the singularity expansion whenever m>1m>1.

S7 Open problems: extended versions

This section presents extended versions of the eight open problems stated in compressed form in Appendix  of the main paper. Each problem includes detailed motivation, relevant background, and suggested research programs.

Problem 1. Uniqueness of the cosine-power profile. Theorem  derives the three formulas – from the cosine-power ansatz and the traveling wave ODE. Proposition  in Appendix  establishes uniqueness within the class of positive, symmetric, single-hump solutions by energy-level analysis in the phase plane. What remains open is the full uniqueness question: whether every compact-support traveling wave of K(m,m) with prescribed speed c>0c>0 takes the cosine-power form, without assuming symmetry or single-hump structure a priori.

A complete proof would rule out asymmetric profiles, multi-hump solutions, and profiles with flat maxima. The phase-plane analysis shows that no such solutions arise on the zero-energy level set, but solutions with different energy levels or topological structure are not excluded by the present argument. Comparison principles adapted to degenerate diffusion equations [13], where compact support arises from analogous mechanisms, may provide the additional tools needed.

Problem 2. Within-class monotonicity and cross-class geometry. The BBM comparison carried out in Main Paper § found BBM solitary waves (N=3N=3, smooth sech2 profiles) about as elastic as K(m,m) compactons (N=5N=5, compact support) by the amplitude measure, with more debris energy; it therefore neither confirms nor refutes the expectation that conservation count alone governs elasticity. The refined Conjecture  posits that monotonicity holds within each geometric class, while interaction geometry may introduce an independent modulation across classes.

Three testing programs would sharpen the picture. Within the compact-support class, equations that possess compact solitary waves but different conservation counts could confirm or refute monotonicity among equations sharing the same tail geometry; candidates include higher-order K(m,n) variants and the Rosenau–Pikovsky equations [16]. A parallel investigation within the smooth-soliton class, testing regularized long-wave equations or Boussinesq-type systems [3] with different conservation counts, would determine whether the BBM–KdV ordering generalizes. Equations spanning additional geometric classes present a third avenue: the Camassa–Holm peakons (cusped, N=∞N=\infty) and equations with algebraically decaying tails offer test cases in which conservation count and tail behavior can be varied independently. Quantitative elasticity-vs-NN curves within each class would convert the conjecture from a qualitative claim into a precise scaling law.

Problem 3. Stability theory for fractional-exponent compactons. Corollary  shows that the mass and the translation generator P=12​I4P=\tfrac{1}{2}I_{4} increase along the compacton family, for all m>1m>1. The standard Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss framework [6, 7] does not convert this into a stability proof: because the K(m,m) Hamiltonian has no quadratic part, the second variation of ℋ−c​P\mathcal{H}-cP at a compacton has infinitely many negative directions, for every m>1m>1 (remark after Corollary  of the main paper). For the fractional regime (m>3m>3), where compacton edges have Hölder regularity C0,αC^{0,\alpha} with α<1\alpha<1 (Main Paper §), stability theory requires extension to function spaces accommodating limited regularity.

The key analytical challenge is defining an appropriate energy functional on a Sobolev-type space that includes compacton profiles with divergent first derivatives at the support boundary. Weighted Sobolev spaces with weights vanishing at the boundary, or Besov spaces matching the Hölder exponent α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1), are natural candidates. Dey and Khare [4] analyzed the stability of K(2,2) using variational methods; extending their approach to K(4,4) and higher would require controlling error terms that diverge at the compacton edge. The cusp case m=3m=3 presents a codimension-one transition where classical and distributional methods meet, and may be the most tractable starting point. The shelf-wave analysis of Main Paper § offers a complementary approach: the smooth solitary waves on positive backgrounds are amenable to standard stability methods, and the singular limit (Theorem ) could provide a regularization pathway for compacton stability by studying the a→0+a\to 0^{+} limit of the smooth stability problem.

Problem 4. Interaction geometry and collision elasticity. Whether solitary wave tail behavior modulates collision elasticity independently of conservation law count is open. BBM solitons, with smooth exponentially decaying tails, interact gradually and perturbatively and collide almost elastically (ℰ≈0.9997\mathcal{E}\approx 0.9997) with only three conservation laws. K(m,m) compactons, whose profiles vanish identically beyond a finite support, interact through abrupt contact and reach comparable elasticity with five conservation laws, while shedding less debris energy (Main Paper §).

The central question is whether interaction geometry can be quantified through a single parameter (the tail decay rate κ\kappa in u⁡(x)∼e−κ​|x|u(x)\sim e^{-\kappa|x|} for smooth solitons, or the regularity exponent α\alpha at the support boundary for compactons) that correlates predictably with collision elasticity at fixed conservation count. The K(m,m) family itself provides a natural testing ground, since the edge exponent α=2/(m−1)\alpha=2/(m-1) varies continuously with mm while the conservation count remains fixed at five. A related question concerns intermediate geometries: do they produce intermediate elasticity? The Camassa–Holm peakons (cusped at the crest but exponentially decaying in the tails) and equations with algebraic tail decay (u∼|x|−γu\sim|x|^{-\gamma}) occupy the geometric spectrum between smooth and compact. Systematic collision measurements across these families would test whether a smooth interpolation between the compact-support and smooth-soliton regimes exists and would provide the empirical foundation for a unified elasticity theory incorporating both conservation structure and interaction geometry.

Problem 5. Master formulas for the full K(m,n) family. The universal formulas of Theorem  apply to the diagonal subfamily n=mn=m. Proposition  in Appendix  shows that the cosine-power ansatz is exclusive to the diagonal: for K(m,n) with m≠nm\neq n and m>1m>1, the mismatch between convection and dispersion powers renders the ansatz inconsistent. Off-diagonal compactons require elliptic-function or more general transcendental profiles.

Within the broader 𝒞N​(m,a,b)\mathcal{C}_{N}(m,a,b) framework of Rosenau and Zilburg [17], additional cosine-power families arise for a≠0a\neq 0. Whether a unified two-parameter master formula α⁡(m,n)\alpha(m,n), ℓ⁡(m,n)\ell(m,n), c⁡(m,n,A)c(m,n,A) can describe the off-diagonal K(m,n) compactons remains open, as does the behavior near the integrable boundary at K(2,1) and K(3,1) [8]. The absolute-value variant |K|​(p,p)|K|(p,p) [5] enlarges the parameter space to non-integer exponents, and the square-wave limit m→∞m\to\infty (where α→0+\alpha\to 0^{+}) represents a natural boundary for the theory.

Problem 6. Approximate integrability frameworks. The classification of Hernández Heredero et al. [8] rules out exact Lax pairs for K(m,m) with real m>1m>1 but does not exclude approximate analogues. Two directions appear promising. First, constructing a formal asymptotic expansion of a Lax-type operator by deforming from K(2,1) = KdV toward K(2,2) through the family ut+(u2)x+(u1+ϵ)x​x​x=0u_{t}+(u^{2})_{x}+(u^{1+\epsilon})_{xxx}=0. Second, seeking a Lax pair involving nonlocal or pseudo-differential operators, hinted at by the structure of the nonlocal conservation law . A complementary numerical approach uses physics-informed neural networks [14] to learn approximate conservation laws directly from K(m,m) solution data. Xing and Charalampidis [19] have demonstrated that neural networks can learn traveling wave solutions of nonlinear dispersive equations, suggesting that data-driven methods may complement the analytical toolkit. More broadly, perturbed NLS equations of the form i​ut+ux​x+|u|2​u=ϵ​f​(u)iu_{t}+u_{xx}+|u|^{2}u=\epsilon f(u) possess finitely many approximate conservation laws whose count depends on the perturbation structure [10]; the constraint-deficit framework predicts that such systems should exhibit quasi-elastic collisions with debris proportional to the conservation deficit, providing a natural test case beyond K(m,m).

Problem 7. Experimental observation of compactons. Three decades of theoretical development have not yet produced a controlled laboratory observation of compacton propagation and collision. The most developed candidate is the granular chain with Hertzian contact interactions [11, 12], where the power-law force law F∝δ3/2F\propto\delta^{3/2} naturally generates nonlinear dispersion. Nonlinear optical media with engineered dispersion profiles [2] offer a second platform where ultrafast measurements could resolve compact pulse profiles and test the quasi-elastic prediction.

Problem 8. Multi-compacton collision asymptotics. The collision theory of Main Paper § addresses pairwise interactions. When NN compactons collide, the five conservation laws must constrain 2​N2N parameters plus a debris field, growing linearly with NN while the constraint count remains fixed. Numerical experiments suggest that well-separated collisions factor into sequential pairwise events [15], but simultaneous three-body collisions have not been studied systematically. Does debris accumulate through repeated collisions? The long-time asymptotics of NN-compacton initial data would test whether K(m,m) dynamics approaches statistical equilibrium or remains dominated by coherent structures, connecting to the broader theory of weak turbulence [18].

S9 Reproducibility

S9.1 Software and environment

All K(mm,mm) simulations are implemented in Python 3.11 using NumPy 1.24 and SciPy 1.11. BBM simulations additionally use SciPy’s solve_ivp with the RK45 integrator. Symbolic verification of conservation law identities and universal formulas uses SymPy 1.13. Figures are generated with Matplotlib 3.8. All code has been tested on Python 3.10 (Google Colab) and Python 3.11 (local, Ubuntu 22.04). A requirements.txt file is included in the repository for reproducible environment setup.

The computational notebook production_multi_m_D3v4.ipynb (included in the repository) runs a finite-difference cross-check of the K(mm,mm) collisions (N=1024N=1024, q=3q=3, δ=0.5\delta=0.5) on Google Colab (Python 3.10, typical runtime: 45 minutes on a T4 GPU instance, or 3 hours on a CPU-only instance). It is not the PSM configuration of Table S2, and its values differ from that table.

S9.2 Code repository

Source code, data files, and Jupyter notebooks are available at:

https://github.com/machyman/kmm-compactons

A tagged release with a persistent DOI (via Zenodo) will be created at the time of publication. The repository contains:

  • •

    papers/hyman2026structure/src/kmm_compactons/: the pseudospectral (PSM) K(mm,mm) solver behind Section  and Figure  of the main paper

  • •

    paper/: figure sources for Figures – and – of the main paper and Figure S1, with their data in paper/ and paper/figdata/

  • •

    src/kmm_solver.py: K(mm,mm) regularized finite-difference solver with dual spectral filtering, used by the cross-check notebook

  • •

    bbm_solver.py: BBM pseudospectral solver

  • •

    collision_analysis.py: Post-collision amplitude extraction and debris spectral analysis

  • •

    shelf_wave_profiles.py: Exact shelf-wave profile computation from quadrature formulas

  • •

    symbolic_verification.py: SymPy scripts for Appendix C verification

  • •

    production_multi_m_D3v4.ipynb: Colab-compatible notebook running the finite-difference cross-check described above

  • •

    tests/: Validation test suite (single-compacton propagation, conservation law verification)

S9.3 Data files

The repository’s data files:

    measurements_D3v4_N1024.json: the finite-difference cross-check run of the notebook above (all four mm values, 30+ measured quantities each), not the PSM data of Table S2

  • •

    BBM_Collision_Results.json: the BBM collision data of Tables S3–S5 (16 rows, 14 distinct configurations; (2,1)(2,1) and (10,5)(10,5) listed twice)
